speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. S. F. TOLMIE (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 84 (from the Senate) to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act.

maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is the purpose of this Bill, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This amendment is for the purpose of increasing the maximum fine from $100 to $300.

maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
At the request of the
province of British Columbia, where the maximum fine is $300.

maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Fine for what?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: For destroying migi'atory birds out of season. Single specimens of some of these birds, such as the trumpeter swan, are worth more than $100, and the idea of increasing the maximum fine to $300 is to strengthen the deterrent effect of this legislation and so prevent the killing of these migratory birds out of season. That is the only change in the Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have no doubt the object is commendable, but, I think, Mr. Speaker, a good deal of discontent will be found in certain portions of the Dominion, particularly on the sea coast, regarding the seasons fixed for prohibiting the shooting of birds. Along the coast our seamen find the privilege of shooting birds is of some value to them, and I am aware of very considerable complaint that the close seasons chosen by the Government in making their regulations have not been wisely chosen. I think that may be dealt with by regulation and does not require any change in the Act, but I bring the matter to the notice of the minister so that if he finds the close seasons have not been well chosen he will have the necessary amendment made.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I understand the season is governed by regulation, but I will be very glad to look into the matter.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1

penalty for violation of Act increased from $100 to $300:

maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is this legislation reciprocal, or are we protecting these migratory birds in order that people in some other country may kill them?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I understand that they
are protected under the Migratory Birds Convention Act passed in connection with the treaty between the United States and this country, and that the legislation is reciprocal.

maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: At the time this Migratory Birds Act was passed there was a great deal of trouble about the provincial and the Dominion jurisdiction over birds, and I have never been able to find out exactly how the question was settled. Can the minister inform us if we now have jurisdiction to deal with migratory birds?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I understand that this
is the treaty between Canada and the United States dealing with this matter:
The ratifications shall he exchanged at Washington as soon as possible, and the convention shall take effect on the date of the exchange of the ratifications. It shall remain in force for fifteen years, and in the event of neither of the high contracting powers having given notification, twelve months before the expiration of said period of fifteen years, of its intention of terminating its operation, the convention shall continue to remain in force for one year and so on from year to year.
In faith whereof, the respective plenipotentiaries have signed the present convention in duplicate and have hereunto affixed their seals.

maintopic: THE MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is not my difficulty at all. The shooting of wild geese in my province, for instance-would that be

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: a matter to be dealt with by provincial law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This legislation is
necessary to implement the Migratory Birds Treaty. There is a special provision in the British North America Act conferring upon Parliament a legislative jurisdiction for the purposes of any law enacted for the purpose of implimenting treaty obligations, whatever may be the subject matter. I think there can be no serious question about the jurisdiction of this Parliament in the matter.

I simply wanted to
have my mind settled on the point.

I rise for two purposes: first, to express a protest against the low tone of voice in which the conversation relating to this Bill is carried on at the far end of the Chamber-in that respect my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, (Mr. Doherty) I must say, is an inveterate sinner

and second, to ask the minister in charge of this Bill if fines are being imposed in the United States similar to those imposed by this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I understand they are,
Mr. Chairman.

That would seem to
be "sound" law.

I am delighted to hear
it. I do wish that some of my other friends on the ministerial benches had the lung power that the Minister if Agriculture has.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House again in committee on Bill No. 116, to amend the Research Council Act and to establish a National Research Institute-Sir George Foster. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this Bill was
last before the committee clause 1 had been adopted with amendments and now appears in the reprinted copy of the Bill. Clause 2 becomes clause 13 of the new Bill.
On section 13-Institute created:
Sir GEORGE FOSTER. I would like to move that section 13, subsection 1, be amended, by inserting after the word "Minister" in the seventh line thereof the words "Governor in Council," and by add-

ing after the word "which" in line 16 the words "subject to the same approval."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 14-duties of Institute:

I move that the following be added as a new section to follow section 14; its number will be 15:
When for the sake of efficiency or economy, or for the purpose of preventing duplication of effort jn the scientific work of the various departments of the Government, or in the scientific work of the various commissions and hoards constituted by the Government, it may be found desirable that such scientific work shall be, either co-ordinated and supervised by, or shall be carried on in whole or in part in the institute under conditions to be approved by the Research Council, appropriate action thereto in each case may be taken by the Research Council when and as directed and empowered by the Governor in Council.
That is to make provision for the purpose, in the first place, of rendering it impossible to have duplication as regards the work of the institute and as regards the work of laboratories which may have been established, and in operation in any of the departments, chiefly with regard to their administrative work; in the second place, of co-ordinating and supervising those existing laboratories and research agencies, so that we may avoid, first, duplication as between themselves and, second, duplication by way of extension of work, heretofore mainly confined to a department, into fields which would take it beyond that administrative work and so encroach upon the work of the institute proper. To summarize: what it aims to do is to prevent the expenditure of money in the duplication of effort, and, in the second place to co-ordinate and supervise all of those agencies so as to bring them into a connected whole. I think it is perfectly fair to do that, because those departments have laboratories more or less extensive, more or less elaborately fitted up, which were designed as subsidiaries and necessary agencies in carrying out their departmental work. For instance, the Health Department has a laboratory system; it makes its own analyses, and ascertains facts and principles, the knowledge of which is needed in the administration of the department itself. But it is quite possible that this might be pushed further than is necessary for that purpose, and it is to bring the supervision of council, the Government itself, into play, so that there shall be co-ordination of effort, not duplication which is costly and uneconomical.

Might I ask the right hon. gentleman to give attention to subclause (f), which reads:
The investigation ana standardization at the request of any of the industries of Canada of the materials which are or may be used in, or of the products of, the industries making such a request.
I am not quite clear as to the purpose and effect of that. Will my right hon. friend give the committee some information as to what will be done under that subclause?

That means
that the Research Institute itself may undertake the investigation and the standardization of materials which go into the processes of the industry, and it may equally investigate and standardize the products of that industry. All that work is done in the interest of economy in the productive process. I do not know whether my hon. friend gets the idea imperfectly, as I have expressed it, hut this is a very important part of the work that is carried on at this institute. Take, for instance, the Mellon Institute in Philadelphia. That institute devotes a very large proportion of attention to this work of investigation and standardization with a vew to economy in production. The United States Laboratory of Standardization and Research, established a little out from the city of Washington, carries on that same form of effort. The same thing is done in researches which have been set on foot in the Old Country.

I am quite sure that the object of the clause and of the Bill generally is an excellent one, and I am not approaching it in any critical spirit. What is the meaning of the word "industry"? Does it mean any particular man doing business? Is he the "industry"? Or has there to be a combination of people in an industry?
This means all the industries of the country, for instance the textile industry or the pulpwood industry.
A textile industry may engage, perhaps, fifty people. Does the expression used in the Bill mean an indi-. vidual? Or does it mean a combination of individuals in one industry?

My hon. friend will see, in a subsequent clause, a reference to trade guilds for research. I think my hon. friend was here the other day
183J
when I read a list of some twenty-four or twenty-six of these trade guilds, which had been formed in Great Britain and which were working in connection with and aided by the British Government in carrying on its central research branch. The same effort will be made here, and I have no doubt that the same method will be followed. For instance, the different lines of industry will be encouraged to form themselves into guilds or associations, such as the textile industry, the leather industry, the boot and shoe industry. Some of them now have associations or guilds with regular membership. The guild itself, or any member through the guild may make application for research work or investigation along any of the lines undertaken by the Research Institute. But that is not meant to shut off any industry which is established and which does not belong to a guild. It will yet have an opportunity of asking for that service from the council, that is the Research Institute; but it will be for the Research Institute, the council, to decide whether it can take up all of those or which of them it should take up-undoubtedly a great many requests will be preferred and it will be impossible to take them all, so that there must be some line of choice as to which would be worth while.

Where there are
guilds, or associations, as suggested by the right hon. gentleman, I can quite understand that the clause might be intelligible. He states that if there is an individual or a firm not in a guild or association, this service would still be open to him or it.
Yes.

I hope so. What is the meaning and effect of "standardization" in this clause? If a particular individual or firm-we will not take the case of a guild-desires to have standardization, and the Research Council is willing to carry it out, what is the effect of that standardization ?

We have now, and have had for two years, an association of engineers who have given their services toward this end, and who are engaged in what they call standardizing the materials and products. What this means, so far as I understand it, is this, that, in reference to materials used in manufactures and the products of manu-

faeturing processes, you may have a hundred different patterns or of different qualities of materials. It may be that a proper process of standardization will eliminate a large number of these and will indicate the kind of material that is best adapted for use in the processes, and may also standardize the patterns and arrange them so as to avoid unnecessary multiplicity of products. The public is just as well served, and the costs of manufactures reduced, because there are fewer patterns and less diffuse material to be used. That committee has been at work for three years. It has no compulsory powers. In the case of any given industry, it makes its investigation, and confers with those in the industry. Already its work has resulted in the adoption by these industries of standard forms. That is a layman's explanation of the matter. I must confess that the subject is a little abstruse for a layman.

We can all understand that standardization, generally speaking, helps in economy, and where all the parties concerned agree on standardization, it is all plain sailing. I suppose this standardization has regard to quality and ingredients as well as to patterns? Let me give an illustration. A manufacturer of cement desires to standardize cement, and submits a formula which is acceptable to the engineers and to the Research Council. It may be very desirable that that should be adopted generally. But other manufacturers of cement may have a different view. What I want to find out is whether this standardization will have any legal effect; will it prevent somebody else from adopting a different method? Has a manufacturer the right to disagree with the council?
The standardization has no compulsory effect. It is there as a sample of what may be worked up to, or what may be worked with, and they adopt it by agreement.
When it suits them.

We have at the present time in the Public Works Department a small laboratory which standardizes cement. They have so standardized it now that men who are contracting with that department for construction work must use that standardized cement.
Was that cement used in the formation of the Union Government?
No, we had a still better cement than that. Competent engineers had previously wrought it out and it has worked splendidly.

I do not wish to oppose this clause, or the Bill, but only to ask the minister a question. I quite understand that the Government wishes to centralize its activities in the scientific domain through an institute of this sort. At present, I understand, individual scientists in the different provinces are able to obtain grants to follow certain lines of research work. Am I right in supposing that they will be deprived of any such help from the Government after this institute is formed? I suppose the minister is ready to give the committee his verbal assurance that when the personnel of this institute is appointed, due recognition will be given to scientists in all lines and from all provinces?
I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension. We are not giving any donations in any way, shape or form, to the different provinces for research work.
I mean to individuals.

No. I will explain. The Advisory Council so far has not had any laboratory: it has had no research equipment of its own. But there is a system of bursaries and studentships and fellowships up to a certain amount. If in the course of his university work a young man has shown an aptitude for a certain line of research work, the Advisory Council, after looking into the matter, may recommend that he be granted a studentship while he is at the university, or a fellowship after he has graduated, to enable him to carry on his particular line of research. That system will not be interfered with in any way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are there any trade guilds for research in any of the industries in Canada at the present time?
They will form as soon as the Research Council is ready for its work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are not existing as yet?

They do not call themselves guilds so far as I know, but all the large industries have their own associations; for instance, the Textile Association, the Boot and Shoe Trade As-

sociation. "Guild " is only another name for association.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15 (inserted as amendment).

The Government is going to be the arbiter, I understand, between the Research Council and the scientific men at present in the service of the Government. Does that mean that the Government will decide as to which scientific men are best qualified to do the work?

In the end it has to come down to a judgment by the Government in all these specific cases. That is true as to the membership of the council itself. By this legislation we are saying that the council -shall consist of so many members, but it must be determined by the Government itself who shall be the members. The Government must take the best means at its disposal to make sure that these fifteen men shall be the very best fifteen men that we can get for the purposes of this Research Council, and that they shall at the same time represent the fundamental interests involved in the work of the Research Institute. There is no other way by which you can get a deciding body. In this case the deciding body is the Government, and the Government must exercise it's best judgment, after such advice as it can get, as to the composition of the council. With reference to the co-ordination of the work of the different laboratories at present in operation, these are all now under the guidance and direction of the Government. There is the minister of the department; he has a staff, and the work comes for ultimate decision to the Government itself. The Government works in that way through its minister. There are three or four departments at least which now have these laboratories, and the Government as a whole, including the ministers of the departments in which the laboratories are situated, must confer as to how they shall carry on, what shall be the supervision, and must take care that there shall be no duplication.

I think
this is a serious mistake. Every organization must have some head, and I certainly do not think that a layman is capable of directing scientific research. I do not believe that the Government should step in and say what researches are to be carried on, and by whom. It seems to me that the final authority in this respect should be
the Research Council. Of course, the selection of the council is quite another thing, and the Government, having got information as regards the qualifications and achievements of certain men, can decide on the personnel. But when it comes to a question of directing a scientific institute, the final authority should not rest with laymen.

The hon. member is quite wrong in assuming that this is going to be done. First we shall have to have the council, and, after that, directors and a staff will be appointed. The Government will not decide, without the advice and recommendation of the council, after a proper investigation, who shall be the directors or who shall carry on different kinds of research. The Government is quite sensible, in the first place, of the importance of having a proper council, but there will be questions arising in which it must assume its responsibility. The Government supplies the money through the regular channels and must therefore have a deciding voice 'in the end. It could not allow the council to say, "We will spend half a million dollars this year on this, that or the other." As we give the money, we must have a voice in its disposition ; but the Government will take scientific advice on scientific matters.

Suppose a conflict
should arise between, say, the Mines Department, and the Research Council, in regard to some scientific research which they both desired to conduct. Who will decide which is to be the final authority?
The Governor in Council; there is no other authority in Canada to decide that.
If a discovery is made by one of the members of the board, how will his personal rights be affected?
We are coming to that later on.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15 (new section 16)-Discoveries and inventions, control of.

I move that
the section be amended by substituting, for the word "Minister" in lines 28 and 29, the words "Governor in Council."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I move to
further amend the section by adding, after

the word "bonuses" in line 33, the words "or royalties."

Where will you get
the money from?

A section that has already been passed constitutes the council a body corporate to receive bequests and donations. This section is subsidiary to that in one respect, and provides a sort of incentive to keep the researchers loyal and attached to the institute, by giving them an interest in any new 4 p.m. process or invention which in the course of their researches, they may discover, either as the final conclusion of a line of inquiry or as incidental to the research. The invention itself becomes the property of the institute, and in proportion to its value, it will be called for and used by industries outside. The industries will then arrange with the institute just the same as they now arrange wiilth any inventor, and upon certain conditions the invention will be made available to those who may wish to use it, on payment of a royalty. To make it worth while for an investigator, who is a paid member of the staff, to follow out to a successful conclusion every lead he hits upon, and to give him in part the benefit of such discovery, the institute will provide a reward in the shape of a royalty on any invention which is made. This it is supposed, will have two good results: there may accrue to the institute itself very considerable sums of money, and there will be collected and kept together a family of researchers in the institute whose interest will be linked with that institute. In this way there will be a better staff and less chance of change.

In other
words, the discoveries will yield sufficient revenues to pay the bonuses; the institute will be ,self-sustaining?

Yes. The
bonuses or royalties can be piatid only out of the fund which is created in the way I have stated.

That is no doubt the
intention, but it might be helpful to suggest in the Bill that the council may pay these bonuses "out of the funds" referred to, or words to that effect. However, if the hon. gentleman thinks it is not necessary, I shall not press the point.

Section 16, -section 17 as it now is-should be amended, when we come to it, by inserting
ff?!r George Foster.]
after the word "donation," at the end of the third line, the words "royalty fees."

What I have in mind, and I presume the minister can clear up any doubts on the point, is this. The proprietor of a certain mine sends a specimen of the ore to this Research Council and they discover a method by which it can be handled at a profit' by that mine owner. Do I understand the minister to say that in a case of that kind the council will fix the royalty to be paid by the person who owns the mine because they have discovered a method of treating the ore which gives the mine its value? .

I do not think such a case comes under "research" such as contemplated here. An industry is carrying on its work-say it is the pulp and paper industry. It meets a certain problem and finds it impossible, with the means at its disposal, to solve that problem. The industry would be greatly benefited and the costs of manufacture largely reduced-if a solution could be found-I have not explained this so far, but I will do so now. The pulp and paper industry-we will say as an instance for the time being-says to the Research Institute, "We want to have a room allocated in the institute with the use of your equipment and with your supervision. We have a man ourselves, we will send him there, and he will apply himself to research work to solve that problem. We will pay all the expenses incurred in helping our research man." If the research man comes upon a valuable discovery, no proceeds of that discovery need be given to the funds of the Research Institute. The discoverer is the pulp and paper industry's own man and they get the benefit of all that their man accomplishes.
The benefit of all discoveries?

Of all discoveries, and they will reward him as they see fit. But in the case of researches carried out by the researchers of the institute themselves, should they happen upon a valuable invention the Research Institute will own the invention and it is to those researchers that the royalty or bonus will be paid. Respecting ore discoveries and other things of the kind, those are more of the nature of analyses-that is not really research work, and is not, I think, germane to this clause.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I suggest
to the minister that there be inserted, after the word "donation" at the end of the third line, the words "royalty, fee".
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.
What will be the annual appropriation for the carrying on of the work of the institute?

That will
depend upon the extent of the equipment and facilities with which we decide to commence. I do not think it is wise for us to start on too expensive a basis, but at the same time we must begin sufficiently well equipped to make the institute really helpful to the industries of the country.
Will the amount appear in the Estimates for this year?

We will bring down the amount-it is under consideration now-in the Estimates, and when it coimes before the House we will be able to give complete explanations as to what we propose to proceed with at first.
On section 17-annual report.

The clause provides that this report shall contain such information and details as "the council and the minister may require." Would it not be better to say "the council or the minister" because if the minister should refuse his assent, the report may not be available to the public? If you accept my suggestion there are two chances to one in favour of the report being published.

I cannot see that there will be any such difficulty as my, hon. friend seems to apprehend. Parliament will get the report fast enough; we will be only too glad to bring it down.
Bill as amended reported, and read the third time and passed.

On motion of Hon. J. A. Calder (Minister of Health) the House went into committee on Bill No. 81 to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act (as amended), Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-prescriptions not to be filled more than once, etc.:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is the Bill as
reported on April 27 last by the special committee to which it was referred for consideration. The only change has been
the addition of subsection (a) of section 1 of the following words:
And by inserting after the word "occasion" in the eleventh line thereof the following words: "except where the preparation covered by the prescription might have lawfully been sold in the first instance without a written order or prescription."
There is no other change in the Bill.

I wish to offer an additional clause to the Bill. The reason I am doing it in this way is that it was thought that this amendment would have to be incorporated in the criminal code, but after consultation with the parliamentary counsel and the minister it was considered wise to insert it in this Bill. It has been found in administering the original Act that light penalties and comparatively small fines had really very little deterrent effect. Therefore I move to amend clause 1 by inserting after paragraph (d) on page 1 of the Bill, the following words:
(d) Subsection 2 of section 5a is amended by striking out the last five lines thereof and substituting therefor the following:
'^Shall be guilty of a criminal offence, and shall be liable upon indictment to imprisonment for any term not exceeding seven years, or upon summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars in costs and not less than two hundred dollars in costs, or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding eighteen months, or.to both fine and imprisonment ; provided that any person who unlawfully sells, gives away or distributes any drug to any minor shall be proceeded against by indictment and not summarily, and, in addition to being liable to the penalty of seven years' imprisonment aforesaid, shall also be liable to be whipped."
That applies only to sale or gift of drugs to minors. I want the committee to realize the seriousness of such an offence. While I have not the definite evidence before me at the present time, I believe my information is accurate, that in many of the large cities drug traffickers actually distribute drugs to high school children or children in the higher grades of the elementary schools for the purpose of stimulating the drug habit among them. A more diabolical and pernicious practice I cannot conceive of. I suggest that in such cases it shall be made possible to apply this severe punishment. I speak from considerable knowledge of conditions in my own city, and I think they are common to other cities as well, that these drug traffickers deliberately traffic in drugs with young girls of sixteen years of age or thereabouts and also with young boys, especially of the clerical and student class, and many

most tragic cases have been brought to light where these young people, especially girls, have been utterly ruined. So I submit to the committee that we cannot make the penalty too severe. I move, therefore, that this amendment be incorporated in the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in 1910, I had the privilege of introducing in this House a Bill for the suppression of the use of habit forming drugs, and I recall receiving representations as to the extent of the traffic. I rise simply to say that what the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has stated is entirely in accord with the information I received at the time. I believe that in the city of Montreal, for example, the nefarious traffic was more or less prevalent at that time, and the legislation then introduced was for the purpose of trying to put an end to it. Apparently it has not been drastic enough, and anything that will help to make it such I should most heartily support.

I am against the idea of
placing on our statute book any provision for the further introduction of whipping. We do not whip people in these days. I admit that there is provision for whipping in the case of certain offences, but this is provided only for cowardly attacks upon weak people. For instance, the penalty of whipping is provided in cases where garrot-ing is resorted to, that is, seizing people on the streets and committing violence upon them. In the case of rape and other offences of violence against women a similar penalty is provided. But the cases to which it is applicable are very few, and, as I say, they are cases of cowardly attacks by the strong upon the weak. In former days people were whipped for almost anything, but the tendency has been to do away with that as far as possible. I would be against the principle of inserting in our laws in this twentieth century penalties of that kind, which have now been almost wiped off our statute book. Then, I think it is a mistake to provide that these offences shall be made indictable offences, the accused not being given an opportunity to elect whether he shall be tried by a magistrate-or in what we call a speedy trial court-rather than by a jury.

My hon. friend is aware that in the case of summary trial the jurisdiction of the magistrate is so limited that in the graver cases of offences it is ineffectual. The idea of the summary trial

was that it should deal with what might be called technical evasions or breaches of the Act, not with the illegal and terrible practice of distributing or using these drugs as has been known to be the case-my hon. friend knows to what I refer. The summary trial was designed to deal with the case of possible oversight on the part of some one dealing in the drug, and the punishment was very mild and very moderate. The only way you can provide for a more severe punishment is by making the offence an indictable one.

An indictable offence is
one in which the accused is indicted and tried before a jury. But if the prisoner wishes to waive his right to trial, by jury, surely the hon. member would not insist that he be tried by a jury willy-nilly. He could be tried before a speedy trial court and get everything that is coming to him there. But if you insist that he shall be tried by a jury you are putting his offence in the same class as treason, murder, and one or two other grave offences. I am not advocating the case of offenders who traffic in these drugs, but I wish to see the symmetry of our law maintained. For that reason I think it would be a mistake on our part to rush into changes of this kind without fairly considering each one of them. I would be positively against that part of my hon. friend's amendment which declares that the offender shall be whipped. That is a relic of past ages which should not be reintroduced into our laws.

I quite
agree with the observation made by the hon. member; I think that the penalty provided is so severe that it will never be enforced, even if sentence under it is made by the court. I think it would be unwise, therefore, to place such a penalty in the law. I would like to ask my hon. friend also whether the age limit 'in this (case is twenty-one years?
Yes.

Well, there are many people around twenty and nineteen years of age who are very wise in the matter of narooties. If the Bill is for the purpose of protecting young and inexperienced persons, I think that the age should be reduced.

Has the hon. gentleman submitted his amendment to the Department of Justice for its opinion?
'Mr. STEVENS:	Yes.

And do they concur
in it?

Yes. I consulted with
the Minister of Justice. The amendment was drafted by Mr. Gisborne, Parliamentary Counsel.

I quite agree with the
view which has been expressed against that feature of the Bill which provides for whipping. I have seen several men whipped, and I think it is an absolutely inhuman practice; we might as well hang the man and be done with it. Possibly the penalty should be increased, but why place such a weapon in the hands of unprincipled people?	Minors-girls, for instance, of
unprincipled character-can make a charge against anybody, with very unpleasant results. There are two sides to these questions. To my mind, when we insert a penalty of this character-
