speechtext: House again in committee on Bill No. 81, to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Stevens has moved an amendment to clause 1, which was under discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Personally I am inclined to the view expressed by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) with reference to the penalty proposed. I doubt very much the advisability of including whipping as a penalty for the offence under discussion. It is quite true

that the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) referred this proposed amendment to the Minister of Justice, but I would judge that the minister approved of it only in form. I have not had the opportunity of discussing the matter with the Minister of Justice, but personally, I would like to see that feature of the amendment struck out. I thoroughly agree with the other provision. Under the law as it now stands, the maximum penalty for the offence referred to is $200. I think that might very well be increased to a maximum of $1,000, leaving it to the magistrate or judge to decide as to what amount up to $1,000 should be imposed in each case.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion. I wish to point out to the committee a few facts. It is quite clear to me that the committee does not appreciate the seriousness of this crime or the prevalence of this pernicious practice of illegally distributing drugs. I do not wish, as it were, to foul my own nest by referring to the Pacific Coast cities, but I am more familiar with the conditions there, and I may add this. I have been giving this question study for a great many years. The hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) mentioned a little while ago that he had brought in a Bill in 1909. I was responsible for the matter being brought to the attention of the then Government. I remember taking some very prominent eastern gentlemen around Pacific Coast cities and showing them the effects of the use of these drugs. They returned to Ottawa and put it up to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the result was the Bill that was introduced by the present leader of the Opposition in 1909.
My hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) a moment ago said that whipping was inhuman. But does not the committee realize that this deliberately conceived illegal distribution of drugs results in the ruination-I am not dealing with imaginary things now, but with cold facts-of scores of young lives, of young girls and young men from the best families, and by "best" I mean morally good. There exists on the Pacific coast-I do not know whether it exists here in the East or not -a highly organized ring of criminals, for the illegal distribution of these drugs. So effective is their organization that the police have been baffled to deal with them in the last few years. I read a brief extract from a report of a meeting held in Vancouver the other day at which Chief of Police Anderson, who has been on the

Vancouver police force for twenty-three or twenty-four years, said that the police were helpless because of the difficulty in getting any penalty commensurate with the crime. Let me give an illustration, a case that occurred within the last month, or witjhin the last two months at all events. A returned soldier named Kehoe, who had rendered excellent service at the front, been wounded and decorated, contracted the drug habit-I do not know how-and he committed a very vicious crime in Vancouver a few weeks ago. The crime was robbery with violence, which my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) mentioned a moment ago. For that offence he got five years and the lash, under the criminal code. My hon. friend said that he does not necessarily approve of that, but that it is perhaps a justifiable course to pursue in some cases. About the same time that this ex-soldier got five years and the lash, there was brought before the magistrate a notorious trafficker in drugs, and under the existing law the magistrate was restricted to imposing a fine and a very, very mild sentence. Now this notorious trafficker in drugs was, I contend, as much responsible for that crime as the ex-soldier himself. This ex-soldier, with an honourable past, had been made a degenerate through the use of drugs. And that is only one case out of hundreds I could mention.
No, no.
My hon. friend (Mr. Currie), with that broad wisdom of his which over-rides the knowledge of everybody else, says "No, no". But I know what I am talking about.

The whole people of
Canada are not "dopes".

I am not suggesting that, and if my hon. friend would suppress his Irish whispers till I finish he could have the floor. I say that the trafficker in the drug was more responsible for the crime than the man who actually committed it, and yet under the law as it now stands it is impossible to give him a sentence anything like commensurate with the crime. The trafficker makes a huge profit,- thousands and thousands of dollars out of a very small quantity of the drug. The difficulty of detecting the smuggling in of these drugs is extreme. They have actually smuggled in the drug from incoming steamers by aeroplane. Traffickers would dump the material overboard with a float, and boats would pick it up. It is exceedingly difficult to detect, although the police are

doing their utmost in every way. But even when the traffickers are caught, they get very light sentences. What I am asking is that as far as ordinary offences are concerned the summary trial should stand, but that in the case of traffickers, these vicious creatures I have been referring to, it should be possible for the#police to indict them, and for the more severe sentence which goes with that method of trial to be imposed. I do not say there should be a fixed term of seven years, but that the maximum should be seven years. Then I go further, and I appeal now to my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) who spoke so eloquently a few moments ago in this regard. He spoke about protecting the weak against the strong. I am appealing to him to support that very principle in the latter part of my amendment. I appeal on behalf of all children and minors, youngsters of the ages of fifteen, sixteen, seventeen and eighteen, scores of whom are annually ruined by this thing. I can tell my hon. friends of actual incidents where young men and young women, with whose families I am personally acquainted, have been utterly ruined by the use of drugs, having acquired the habit through the agency of these particular parasites I have mentioned. Against that crime of giving drugs to children and minors I say that not only is imprisonment necessary, but it should be made possible for a judge and jury in their discretion to add the lash. This amendment does not make it compulsory, but it provides that in severe cases there shall at least be some method of dealing with this heinous offence. My closing word to the committee is this: If it so happens that hon. gentlemen have not had personal experience with this class of crime, I suggest that they pause before treating the matter lightly, and bear in mind these statements which I have made, and which may be substantiated fully both by officials in the administration of the law and by other authorities as well. It is proposed to call, for May 12, a conference of representatives of all the coast cities to secure amendments to the criminal code just along the lines I am mentioning; but any action taken will be too late for this year, and another year will go by before any relief can be secured. I therefore ask the committee to give this matter very serious consideration. As my hon. friend said a moment ago, the principal idea is to protect the weak and innocent, and it is also important that we should make adequate provision against the heinous crime of trafficking in drugs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When I spoke a moment ago I was speaking entirely from memory, but since then I have had an opportunity of referring to Hansard of the time at which this subject was debated. It was in January, 1911, during the session of 1910-11, that the legislation was passed. What I had particularly in mind, in referring to the city of Montreal, were the representations made at the time by some of the officers in charge of the Children's Aid work in that city. I find I said to the House that the Probation Officer of the Children's Aid Society had given this subject very careful study, and had reported that of her own observation she had met as many as fifty or sixty little girls and boys within the same day, in the city of Montreal, all of whom had acquired the cocaine habit to some degree. I remember having had an interview with this officer before introducing the legislation, and I was so astonished at the representations made that I took occasion to communicate with a large number of responsible citizens in Montreal, including the heads of a number of different religious denominations, settlement workers, and others. The communications received from them will be found in Hansard of January 26, 1911, at page 2525, and three or four pages following. If hon. members have any doubt about the representations made by
5 p.m. the member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), they will, on perusal of these statements, discover that he is entirely correct. I do not think there is a class of evil that is more vicious in its possibilities than the attempt to have young children acquire the drug habit, and if there are any fiends of this kind abroad in the community, it seems to me that, if the money penalty or imprisonment is insufficient to restrain them, Parliament should provide more drastic measures.

I think
the House will agree that in regard to the cases referred to by the member for Vancouver there can be no great difference of opinion. Personally, I would advocate penalties going almost to any limit to restrain people who force others into the drug habit. But I do not think that there is much to be gained by flogging; apart from this, I would support any penalty at all in cases of this kind. However, I must, as I did the other day, object to this clause in the Bill. I sometimes think that we have acquired a sort

of mania for restricting and restraining people. I have said that before, and I say it now. In very many ways now, a man does not know whether, according to law, he is a law-abiding citizen or a criminal. We are passing laws one year and repealing them the next. Now, I objected the other day on behalf of the ordinary man or woman who is forced back to the mediical man to get ordinary household prescriptions refilled. I do not object to punishing the drug fiend, and f;he penalties in this respect may be made as extreme as is desirable.. But I am absolutely opposed to this eternal attempt to restrict the liberties of the ordinary man. I do not think that this provision is required; it is not wanted by medical men, I am quite sure of that; and it is also an insult to druggists. Furthermore, it is a restriction of the liberties of the great mass of the people. I should like to see some means adopted whereby the case of these drug fiends can be differentiated from the case of ordinary law-abiding people who should have some freedom in the matter of having prescriptions refilled. Many people have household remedies which they have been getting refilled year after year for years, and this liberty will be absolutely restrained if this Bill is passed as it is. It is not fair that nine hundred and ninety-nine inen should be penalized on account of the thousandth. I am of the opinion that outside of the great cities of Canada there are practically no drug fiends in the country. I do not hesitate for a moment to accept the statement of the hon. member for Centre Vancouver that the drug habit is a grave problem in his part of the country. It is also, no doubt, a serious problem in Montreal, and perhaps in other large cities. But out in the rural parts of the country, which, after all, constitute the greater portion of Canada, the drug habit is practically unknown. I again register my protest against this legislation, and while I absolve the minister-because I know that a great deal of it is put into his hands by the departmental officials-I think that this House should seriously take into consideration whether the Civil Service of the country should prepare and mould all legislation of this kind, or whether Parliament should have a greater share in the shaping of it. At any rate, I think the application of this law should be such as not to interfere with the rights and liberties of the people in the rural and smaller urban centres. I agree with 
the member for Centre Vancouver that everything should be done to curb the drug habit, and no penalty is too great for men who will commit crimes such as he has recited this afternoon. But, after all, there are others to be considered too; and while any further protest on my part may do no gogd, I am going to voice my objection once more to all restrictive measures of this kind. I have objected in the past, and will continue to do so as long as I am a member of the House.

I regret to hear of the prevalence of the drug habit in portions of British Columbia. I had observed previous to the war that there was a little weakness in the political mentality of that province. I did not think, however, that the drug habit there had gone so far as to be responsible in any degree for that political mentality.
They were chloroformed.

That point on one side, I am disposed, in the matter of the lash, for this offence, to agree for once, in a way, with my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). I remember that a crime known as garroting becoming very prevalent in the neighbourhood of London. It was a peculiar form of the crime of robbery with violence, and the favorite victims of garroters were found, for a period, to be old people. In that case the cat-o'-nine-tails was applied with very great benefit to the community, and the practice of garroting disappeared with very great rapidity. But I distinguish between that crime and even so reprehensible an action as the sale of drugs. In the case of garroting there was crime with violence which absolutely took away the liberty of the victim. In the case of the sale of drugs there is, to some extent, the agreement of the victim who buys the drugs. Now while the cat-o'-nine-tails is a good implement for crimes of the gravity of garroting, I agree with my hon. friend from North Simcoe that it is doubtful whether the community will not in the long run be affected in a worse degree by the example of the Government along the line of what, after all, is a brutal proceeding, than by the prevalence for some period of this drug habit and of the conduct of the people who minister to it in commerce. Having made that exception, I agree with all who have spoken that the punishment, along the line of imprisonment, should be as severe as ordinary humanity would permit

ns to inflict; but I doubt very much whether we should/ allow the whip, or physical punishment, in even so serious a case as this.

I wish to say a word or two along the lines expressed by my hon. friend from Red Deer and other hon. gentlemen who have spoken, that the lash should generally be kept for crimes which are in the nature of the crimes of a bully- that is the crime of wife-beating, the crime of cruelty to children; I mean physical cruelty to children. While I agree absolutely with my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver in regard to the great criminality of the people who administer and sell these drugs, at the same time I think, and doubtless he will agree with me, that if you make the imprisonment penalty and the fine penalty, particularly the former, severe enough you will probably accomplish what he seeks to accomplish by the use of the lash. I understand that the punishment now for this crime is something like imprisonment for one year, and I think his amendment will probably be a perfectly wise amendment if he leaves out the lash. If I happen by any chance to be a member of this House one, two, or three years from now, after the more severe imprisonment penalty has been tried, and if at that time it is found that the imprisonment penalty has not brought about the cessation of this traffic in drugs, at which he aims, then I think his suggestion might be considered. In the meantime I believe it would be wise to leave the lash for the punishment of a few other crimes which it is used for, or proposed to be used for, at the present time. '
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: According to this proposition the burden of proof is thrown on the accused in the event of a drug being found in his place or on his person; he has to prove that the drug has been put there without his authority or consent. Now, such a drug might be found in the house of a man who was acting in perfectly good faith and who was ignorant of its presence. It is very difficult sometimes for a person to prove his innocence, and it is contrary to English law to regard a man as guilty unless his guilt is proved,- the accused does not have to prove his innocence. I think such a provision should be omitted from the clause.

If I am in order I would like to move an amendment to the amendment presented by my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver, and it is to this effect:
To strike out the words "and in addition to being liable to the penalty of seven years imprisonment aforesaid shall also be liable to be whipped."
That is to say I would be prepared to accept the amendment with the words I have just mentioned struck out. By the amendment, it will be noted, the term of imprisonment is increased to seven years, the fine is raised to $1,000 maximum and the minimum is $200. I think that ought to satisfy even my hon. friend from Vancouver for the present.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As now proposed to be amended the amendment will read:
"shall be guilty of a criminal offence, and shall be liable upon indictment to imprisonment for any term not exceeding seven years, or upon summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars and costs and not less than two hundred dollars and costs, or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding eighteen months, or to both fine and imprisonment; provided, that any person who unlawfully sells, gives away or distributes any drug to any minor shall be proceeded against by indictment and not summarily."
The question is on the sub-amendment.

There are some persons-happily for the world not many, but I suppose in all communities there is the possibility that there are a few-of such a brutal nature that they are not to be brought to justice by any of the ordinary means of law. In these few cases there is abundant reason for using the lash, but such cases ought to be very few, and I am not clear that the case made out by the hon. member for Vancouver is a proper one. Even if the evil which he describes is less than he pictures, it is still a very great evil and should be dealt with by the House in all gravity and seriousness. But I have difficulty, I confess, in quite understanding how this evil of trafficking in drugs with children can be as broad as is alleged, These drugs are expensive, nobody can afford to give them away to school children; and the opportunities of detection would become very large indeed if you dealt with school children-grown persons can be parties to concealment but children cannot very well be so. It seems to me that if the evil is as broad as my hon. friend describes it, it would be much more easily detected than, from his observations, we might judge. Then as to the question of cost, I cannot see where any drug fiend can have any object in spending his money in giving these drugs away to children. I am afraid that aspect of the question is somewhat magnified. But even if it existed in a lesser degree it would merit severe punishment.

Then there is another thought. My hon. friend's amendment deals with a minor. Now a child and a minor are not really quite the same. A young man of twenty years and eleven months is a minor, and a young woman of the same age is a minor; but we know they are both capable of understanding things, and I do not think it is right, in such a matter as this, to treat all persons below twenty-one years of age as being children. Young men of nineteen or twenty, and young women of the same age, have arrived at years, if not of discretion, of understanding, and I do not think we should treat them as children. For all these reasons, while' I will support my hon. friend very heartily as to the general character of his amendment, I think the whipping provision had better be omitted.

A good many laws
have been placed on the statute books which, to my mind, in the punishment prescribed, have been unjust, illogical and unreasonable. There is no getting away from the fact that a discrimination has been made in favour of those who possess wealth, and that these might commit a crime and receive practically no punishment while a poor person who committed the same crime might be very severely dealt with. To illustrate what I mean I may take the case of two men who have violated the law by getting drunk.
Same hon. MEMBERS : Oh, oh.

I see, hon. gentlemen laugh at the idea of any person getting drunk in these dry times. The two men come before the magistrate, who convicts them and prescribes so many days or so many dollars as punishment. The man who has plenty of wealth simply hands out his dollars and walks home; the other poor fellow, having probably spent all his money in liquor, goes to jail. That seems to me to be unreasonable and illogical. But coming to the punishment of drug traffickers, my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Jacobs) thinks we should be satisfied if we impose the maximum penalty of seven years' imprisonment and $1,000 fine. Well, if the culprit has lots of money the mere payment of $1,000 will not amount ,to very much in the way of punishment. But the seven years' imprisonment is supposed to have a certain deterrent effect upon that man and others like him. So far so good. If, in addition to imposing the penalty of imprisonment, you can reach some of those creatures by applying the lash, then apply

it by all means. On general principles I would apply the lash to all of them. It might not have any effect on some of them, but even if it deterred only a few from repeating the crime the lash would be justified. I have not the slightest sympathy for the person who traffics in these drugs. We think it quite right to apply the lash to a brute who beats his wife, but I can imagine no more brutal character than he who coolly and deliberately plans, for his own financial gain, to absolutely ruin the lives of his fellow-citizens. Does that individual deserve one particle of sympathy or consideration? There is only one feature to look at in applying the lash, and that is, will it have a brutalizing effect on the man who applies it? If you say it will, some consideration might be given to the objection to this form of punishment, but none so far as its effect on the creature who traffics in drugs is concerned; the law cannot be too severe upon him. Why restrict imprisonment to seven years? What is the use of letting a creature of that kind out after seven years? He is better behind the bars for his natural life. If in the course of time he reforms, then you might give him another chance, but on general principles I think it would be safer to keep the brute in prison. The lash will have a deterrent effect, I believe, upon these criminals who are cowards in their nature, and for that reason the punishment should be made applicable to them, because any person who for the sake of his own gain will plot to destroy his fellow-human beings is the most cowardly creature I can imagine.

When we had this matter up in the House at the time of the original enactment, the question arose as to making this trafficking in drugs an indictable offence, but the hon. member for Durham (Mr. RoWell) thought it was absolutely necessary that the magistrates be given summary powers in order that they might deal quickly with these cases. Now, the amendment as proposed makes the trafficking an indictable offence, and the penalties both as to fine and imprisonment are more severe than if the case is dealt with under the sections relating to summary procedure, and there is no doubt that a guilty man will elect to proceed under the latter and thus defeat the purpose we have in view. I would like the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) to express his opinion in regard to the right of election. I think that under the amendment as it stands now the accused would have the

right to elect whether or not he would be tried summarily or by a court of competent jurisdiction-I cannot give, offhand, the wording of the section.

The amendment, as I
understand, declares that hereafter this trafficking is to be an indictable offence.
That is just the point -whether he will be tried by a magistrate under the summary conviction section or will elect to be tried by a court of competent jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the first place, it may be pointed out that so far as this special provision in regard to minors is concerned, the summary method of procedure is absolutely excluded. While I am not prepared to answer offhand, being like my learned and hon. friend without the text of the law before me, I must confess that my impression would be that the choice would not necessarily rest with the accused. It would strike me that if you give him in a case of this kind absolute choice you enable him to make inapplicable the higher penalties that are imposable where the proceedings are upon indictment. I do not wish to speak too positively, but my present impression is that it would be open to the prosecuting authority to proceed by indictment. It is not a question, I think, of particular application in this particular case; it is a question of the application of the general principles of the Criminal Code that have to do with proceeding by indictment or upon summary conviction. Speaking from recollection, I think there are certain classes of cases where the election is given to the accused, and that, say, in the cases where the election is so given to the accused, with a formula just as this formula is, it would be open to the prosecution, if they thought the gravity of the case was such that it ought to be possible to impose the greater punishment that might follow on the trial by indictment, to proceed in such manner that the case would be tried upon indictment.

My recollection is that
there is not much doubt that the accused has the election in this case. There are certain cases in which the jurisdiction is absolute. There are certain provinces in which the jurisdiction is absolute so far as the magistrate is concerned. We have cases now before us in which there is a dispute between different provinces as to whether the magistrate has jurisdiction or not, and I think that is one point that ought to be
put beyond all question of doubt. But as as it is, the magistrate must ask the accused in the box whether he is ready to be tried by him summarily or to be tried before a court of competent jurisdiction, and if that is the case the effect of the Act would be defeated.

It seems to me that in
applying penalties of this kind some progressive system should be adopted. For instance, suppose a man is charged with breach of the law, he is tried and convicted and a minor penalty imposed. If he appears before the court a second and a third time, then the penalty which the hon. gentleman has in mind should apply. Otherwise, I question whether it is fair to leave the door open to blackmail as miight be the case under such a clause as this. Now, I have had some experience in matters of police work; in my younger days I was a reporter for the Mail and Empire for something like ten years, and I have a pretty fair idea of the number of cases of this kind that might occur. It seems to me that we are wasting too much time over trifles. From the time that we are taking over this thing and the speeches we are making and the efforts we are putting forth, the public might naturally come to the conclusion that the whole country is seething with this drug evil. As a matter of fact, such is not the case. No country in the world is freer from drug fiends than Canada is, and we are legislating for perhaps one case in fifty thousand. In doing this, we are, to my mind, blackening the character of the great majority of the people of this country, and I do not see that there is any necessity for it. In the first place, a man does not become a trafficker in the eyes of the law until he has had a conviction or two registered against him and penalties imposed of a minor character. If he becomes a trafficker, having been convicted once or twice, then let the major penalty apply. I have seen many cases where innocent men have been badgered by legislation of this kind. If you pass such drastic legislation as this, you are putting a weapon into the hands of irresponsible and wicked people to blackmail honest people. I have watched with a great deal of interest the trend of legislation in this House so far as drugs are concerned. A druggist to whom I was talking recently protested against this repeated legislation. He is an honourable man, who does not traffic in drugs or anything of the kind, and he said that if we kept on passing laws in the House of Commons with reference to

drugs, the stage would very soon be reached where if a mother looked at her son's tongue in the morning, found that he was not feeling very well, and said to him: "Johnny, you ought to go and take a dose of salts," she would be liable to ten years' imprisonment and the whip. We are going to absurd lengths in this matter. Why should we waste time legislating for one case in fifty thousand, as we are doing this afternoon? There are so-called social service workers who are magnifying the effects of these drugs in order that they may draw good salaries; that is about the size of it. When I was a reporter I reported all the criminal cases, and I must confess that nine hundred and ninety-nine people in a thousand are free from any crime, and that no country is as free from it as Canada is. I object to any legislation which would make one think that Canada is populated by drug fiends. For that reason I think that this clause should be modified to provide that a man may not be indicted for the first offence. If we leave it as it is, the result may be the indictment of a man who never saw a drug as contemplated in this Act. A dissolute woman, regardless of justice or fair play, might impugn the character of an honest man, a clergyman or some one who had called upon her; she might lay a charge against him, and if he had lots of money he would have to pay. Let us apply some common sense to our legislation. Let us not be a nation of uplifters; there is far too much hypocrisy in all this legislation. I think, therefore, that this clause should be allowed to stand for another day in order that the Minister of Justice may give it further consideration with a view to the drafting of a sane provision which we can adopt here without feeling ashamed of it after we leave the House.

Some months ago three or four trunks of cocaine were seized by officers of the Crown in Montreal and put in the Court House. A few days afterwards, when the case was about to be proceeded with before the criminal Court, the Court House was broken into during the night and the cocaine disappeared. I am informed that the Government are aware of the location of the cocaine. Have any proceedings been taken in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not personally
cognizant of the matter. Such proceedings as are referred to would be taken under the direction of the officers of the Department of Health. Of course, they might appeal

to us to provide professional assistance. I only mention this to explain why the matter has not come to my knowledge in any way. I shall, however, make inquiries either through the officers of the Department of Health or through my own officers so far as they may have been in connection with the matter, and give the hon. gentleman the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The matter was brought to my attention for the first time last night when I got simply a hint that something of that kind had occurred. I did not get the details the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) has just given to the committee. However, I gave instructions to have a statement of the facts in connection with that case prepared for me, and I expect to have the information at any time.
Surely if the cocaine is located, it will remain in the hands of the officers of the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes.
Amendment to the amendment (Mr. Jacobs) agreed to.
Amendment (Mr. Stevens), as amended, agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for Laurier and Outremont (Mr. Du Tremblay) referred to paragraph (d) of the Bill which deals with the question of possession of these drugs, and he thought it very unreasonable that the party in whose premises these drugs might be found should be called upon to prove that they were there lawfully. I might just read to the committee a memorandum that was placed in my hands by the department regarding the difficulties which they have had in connection with that portion of the law:
The reason for this amendment is due to the fact that in the enforcement of the Act it has been found that the magistrate in the courts of various provinces have interpreted the word "possession" as mentioned in this section to have very many different meanings or intentions, for instance one magistrate in the province of British Columbia gave as his opinion that the word "possession" meant that a person to be in possession must be the absolute owner, and be able to dispose of the property to the exclusion of all other persons, while as a matter of fact, in most cases, persons found in possession of these drugs are only the agents (or intermediates) for the real owner. These persons, however, found in actual possession of these drugs are the ones who are of course responsible for the illegal carrying and distribution of the same. It might be further explained that in many cases where the police search the premises and find in a room occupied by a Chinaman or other person, quantities of opium, etc., and where the accused is charged

with having the drug in his possession, the defence is offered that the drug is not the property of the accused, having been left there by some unknown person. It will therefore be observed that it is very important that the meaning of the word "possession" in so far as it pertains to this section should be defined as clearly as possible for the guidance of the magistrates who have to deal with these cases.
In other words, in carrying out the administration of the law, the department,
1	am advised, in case after case, fell down in their prosecutions simply because they were not able to prove that the person who was in possession of the drug actually owned the drug. For that reason, this amendment was suggested, and I have no doubt at all, that if approved by the committee and carried by the House, it will aid very materially in the administration of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I beg to move to amend sub-clause (e) of clause 1 by substituting for the word "the" in the sixth line on page
2	of the Bill the word "a". The clause will thus read:
the certificate of a Dominion analyst as to the result of analysis.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In clause 7, line 19, there is a phrase, the meaning of which is not quite clear. The clause reads:
And if such drug is there found bring it before a magistrate having jusrisdiction in the matter.
Does that mean to bring the drug or the possessor of the drug before a magistrate? If the drug is to be delivered to a magistrate, should the clause not read:
If such drug is there found deliver it to a magistrate having jurisdiction in the matter.
Either it is the possessor of the drug who is to be brought before a magistrate, or it is the drug which is to be delivered to a magistrate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The explanation of the form of words which, at first glance, might appear to be more applicable to a person than to a thing, is not improbably this, that if you say that he is to deliver the drug to a magistrate, you put upon the magistrate the obligation, under all circumstances and under any conditions, to take possession of the drug and hold it, whereas the drug so found being brought before a magistrate, the circumstances may, in the judgment of the magistrate, he such that he may make some other order
in regard to the drug. While the expression may not be a very elegant one, it produces the same result in that it brings the drug to the magistrate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that the intention?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. There are other provisions with reference to persons being brought before a magistrate.
What will the magistrate do with the drug?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Under the old law these drugs which were taken to and left with a magistrate were formerly disposed of by him. We propose now that, all these drugs, when seized, shall be taken to a magistrate, and when the cases are disposed of, the drug, instead of being disposed of by the magistrate, shall be forwarded to the minister at Ottawa to be disposed of by him. That provision appears in clauses 8 and 9 of the Bill, the two new clauses which were inserted in the Bill for the purpose of correcting that difficulty in the old law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The words which the minister has just used "take it to the magistrate," would be better than the words "bring it before the magistrate."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Probably.

Does the
minister purpose taking power to remit penalties if, upon investigation, it is thought desirable to do so? If, for instance, a magistrate imposed a penalty against a party and it afterwards transpired that the conviction was made upon improper evidence, would the minister have power under any of these amending clauses to make a remission? I have a case particularly in mind. I am sorry to occupy the time of the committee by referring to it here, but it might save a visit to the minister. In a certain town in the province of Nova Scotia-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It might save time if I simply stated that there is, as I understand it, under some general statute, power given to the Governor in Council to remit fines or penalties. There is no such power in this Act. As to the particular case the hon. member has in mind, that matter was dealt with under the general statute the other day, and I understand that provision has been made for a remission of the penalty.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: Application was refused.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was under consideration. As a matter of fact, action has been taken in that case, and there has been a remission, I think, of the greater portion of the penalty.

Then I was misinformed. I had a letter from one of the departments advising that the application was refused, and I could not understand it, because it did seem a case where it was unfair to insist on the full penalty.

I would point out to the Minister of Justice that there is something lacking, in the amendment of my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). I see no provision made in case the man fails to pay the fine. There is a general provision on the statute book that in case of default in payment of a fine, there shall be a term of imprisonment not exceeding three months, but I do not suppose that that would be regarded as sufficient if a man failed to pay a fine of $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As it reads, he may be sentenced to a fine of not less than $200 and costs, or to imprisonment to a term not exceeding eighteen months, or to both fine and imprisonment. It seems to me
Those are substantive punishments. They do not cover the case where the man fails to pay the fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There would be no
harm perhaps in adding some words to make that clear, although my impression would be-

It is not a question of " no harm." These are separate punishments, each of them; they are not alternative. There is no punishment for not paying the fine. We have a statute that provides in case of default, in the payment of a fine a man may he sentenced to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, but I suppose that would not be considered sufficient in this case. I only bring that to the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) informs me that this section was drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel, and that the very question which the hon. member now raises was considered, and that he was advised by the Parliamentary Counsel that the general provisions of the Criminal Code providing for imprisonment in default of
[Mr. Calder.j
a method of enforcing payment of a fine would, without special reference to them here, find their application in this particular instance. The hon. gentleman is quite clear in his impression that imprisonment is limited to three months?
" Not exceeding three months " is the exact language.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of a general provision. It would seem that there ought to be a provision for a longer imprisonment than that, if that be quite correct. Perhaps I might suggest this: if the Bill be allowed to go through committee now, I will have the precise situation verified, and if there be need to add something to this, as the hon. member suggests, and as I confess looks to me probable at the moment, the hon. minister will see that the Bill be recommitted for the purpose of making the addition.
I did not want the promoter of this amendment to be taken by surprise later ton, and to find that in cases where the fine was not paid the alternative was only three months' imprisonment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I fully appreciate the value of the suggestion, but I think we might see it adequately met in the manner I have just mentioned.
Bill as amended reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the motion of Right Hon. Mr. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 12, to amend and consolidate the law relating to copyright, was read the second time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A number of hon. members are interested in this Bill, the second reading of which has just been carried. It is a Bill which I think it would be most desirable should be referred to a special committee, to be there studied and reported back to this House. Many of the provisions of the Bill are of a highly technical nature, and I therefore think we are making no mistake in adopting that course. I therefore had the intention to move that it should be referred to a special committee, and I shall make that motion as soon as we have agreed upon the names of the hon. members who shall compose that committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The reason I did not speak on the second reading was that it was my understanding that it was the intention of the minister to have this

Bill referred to a special committee. It is partly in the nature of a consolidation, and partly in the nature of amendments. I think it is important that the committee should clearly distinguish between the two, and that the House should be fully informed, when the Bill comes before it again, what are the amendments that are proposed as distinguished from the consolidation. I think the Bill also involves conflicting interests to a certain extent, as between publishers and authors, and I should hope that the committee might find it possible to reconcile those differences as far as may be.
There is one further feature that I think should be mentioned, and that is that the Bill has an international significance, and that as it stands it is open to the possibility of occasioning retaliatory legislation. I hope the committee will carefully consider that feature also when the Bill is referred to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman has very clearly indicated the reasons which justify our referring the Bill to a Special Committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does the right hon.
minister now move that the Bill be referred to a Special Committee to be subsequently named?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?

Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Acting Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 118, to amend the Bankruptcy Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Would the minister state
briefly what is the principle involved in this Bill?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do not think that I could describe these amendments as involving any particular principle. They are
184J
drawn with the view of clarifying some of the sections which are considered more or less doubtful in their present form. There are no radical changes in the Bill as originally presented, and all the amendments, I think, have been suggested by financial associations, such as the bankers, trust companies, who are for the most part trustees in bankruptcy, the Association of Chartered Accountants, and the retail and wholesale mercantile associations. There are a great many amendments and many of them are rather elaborately drawn. Many of the sections in the present Bill are to repeal existing clauses, although there has been very little change in language in the repealing clauses. It has been felt that it is better to have a new clause rather than change a few words here and there in the old clause, because it would be easier of interpretation in the courts, or in offices, in its amended form than it would be if we merely insert a few words here and there. I think the best way is to explain the Bill clause by clause as we progress in committee.
_ Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On clause 3-"Available Act of Bankruptcy".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the minister explain what is involved in that substitution?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The paragraph of the former Act which we propose to repeal reads as follows:
"available Act of Bankruptcy" means an act of bankruptcy available for a bankruptcy petition at the date of the presentation of a petition on which a receiving order is made.
The new proposed paragraph enlarges that definition by providing three subsections :
(a) "available act of bankruptcy" means an act of bankruptcy committed within six months before the date of (1) the presentation of a bankruptcy petition, or (2) the making of an authorized assignment, or (3) the payment, delivery, conveyance, assignment, transfer, contract, dealing or transaction mentioned in section thirty-two of this Act."
Mr. du TREMBLAY: Why do you give six months?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well, six months was considered a reasonable time, to establish the fact that an Act done within six months of the presentation of a petition was done in contemplation of bankruptcy difficulty.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-"Local newspaper".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the change there?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The old section read as follows:
"Local newspaper'' means a newspaper published in and having a circulation throughout the bankruptcy district or division wherein the debtor has resided or carried on business for the longest period during the six months immediately preceding the date of the presentation against him of a bankruptcy petition or the making by him of an authorized assignment.
Now the words that are left out are:
"wherein the debtor has resided or carried on business for the longest period during the six months immediately preceding the act of bankruptcy."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-"person".

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The object of this
amendment is that it has been doubted whether, under the wording of the present Act, the definition of "person" was broad enough to include an incorporated bank for certain purposes under the Act, particularly in regard to proving claims as a secured creditor; and secondly, whether it was broad enough to include a trust company for the purpose of having such company appointed a trustee in bankruptcy. The new clause has been broadened for the purpose of including both an incorporated bank and a trust company for these purposes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6-dismissal of petition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would explain each of these substitutions as we go along.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The reason for this is to use the more imperative form. The present section reads as follows:
If the court is not satisfied with the -proof of the petitioning creditor's debt, or of the act of bankruptcy, or of the service of the petition, or is satisfied by the debtor that he is aible to pay his debts, or, in ease an authorized assignment has been made, that the estate can be best administered under the assignment, or that for other sufficient cause no order ought to be made, it may dismiss the petition.
The desire is to make that read "it must dismiss the petition" as being rather more imperative than the word "may."
That leaves no discretion at all?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No discretion under the circumstances which are enumerated in section 6. It is to avoid the possibility of filing a petition in court for the purpose of annoying the trader.

Have there been any
cases of that kind before the courts?
IMr. Mackenzie King.]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do not know that
there has been a decision on the point but it has been suggested that we should give authority to the court whereby the petition under these circumstances could be dismissed.

It seems we ought to give the Act a chance to function and if we find that any abuses arise it will then be time to make a change. But merely changing the Act for the sake of change does not appeal to me as being the proper thing to do.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-commencement of bankruptcy.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Under the old section the time dated from the service of the petition. In a great many cases you cannot effect service. It is a very slow process, as a debtor may leave his ordinary place of business or ordinary residence. The time, under the amendment, will count from the date of the presentation to court of the petition.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-receiving order or assignment to be filed.
Would the minister please explain the original section?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There was no provision in the original section as to where these documents should properly be filed, and it is with the idea of fixing a definite place for the filing of the petition that this amendment is introduced.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-affidavit upon registration where- title to real estate or lien affected.
Will you explain that also?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In Alberta, in Saskatchewan, and in the portion of the province of Ontario which is under the Land Titles system difficulty has arisen in registering bankruptcy proceedings against the particular lands which are affected. The officials of the courts in these provinces have therefore requested that provision be made whereby the bankruptcy proceedings may be registered as notice against the particular real estate which is to be affected. With that end in view this amendment has been made.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 10-trustee to convene meeting of creditors on proposal for composition, extension or scheme of arrangement:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The new section proposes to extend and to more definitely fix the duties of trustees and others in regard to meetings of creditors. The essence of the changes made to this section is the grant of power to creditors, in case a proposal for a composition, extension or scheme of arrangement is made before the making of a receiving order or an authorized assignment, to carry on the business of the debtor under a committee, with grant of power to the court to hold off all creditors who are attempting to realize independently until it is discovered whether the proposal will or will not be accepted. This applies to sections 10, 11 and 12 of the present Bill which are drawn for that general purpose land to take the place of similar provisions not so fully elaborated in the Act as it stands to-day.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-proposal of composition or arrangement before receiving order or assignment has been made, etc.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This is an attempt
to supply what was a real defect in the Bankruptcy Act passed two sessions ago. It provides entirely for proceedings which in Great Britain would take place under the Deeds of Arrangement Act. It is in order to avoid bankruptcy and enable the creditors and the debtor to get together to make a composition, to grant an extension of credit, or to make an arrangement of the debtor's affairs. If at such meeting an arrangement to avoid bankruptcy is come to, all the proceedings to carry that arrangement into effect are set out dn the amendment proposed by section 11. That was an omission in the former Act.

I notice that provision is made for the payment of reasonable costs to the trustee for his services. While I have no objection to the trustee receiving reasonable costs, I would point out that in the present Act the costs are fixed at a certain figure, five per cent.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This is more in the nature of a private arrangement before any act of bankruptcy; in the other case we fixed the costs where there was an act of bankruptcy. It is hardly the same.

In subsection 3d I notice that sufficient proof of a debt due to the creditor can be made by cable or telegraphic communication. It seems to me that opens
the door to some considerable abuse. Is the proof thus submitted to be supplemented by formal proof later?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We could put in the words "shall for the purposes of the said meeting". I do not want to make it too difficult before acts of bankruptcy. The creditor has to prove claims to enter into this arrangement. The desire was to simplify it as much as possible.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I would move to add after the word "Act" on the last line of the page the words "for the purposes of such meeting".

But suppose there is no further meeting? Suppose the creditors agree to accept the offer made and the only proof of a heavy debt is a mere cable communication. It seems to me that the trustee or person in charge ought to have some supplementary proof that this debt actually exists.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think the ordinary provisions of the Act in regard to proof would apply. The cable communication would be strictly limited to the purposes of the meeting; it would not be proof of claim.

It would be
proof of claim for the purposes of the meeting, and if a cable communication is received from a party stating that he has a very large claim, that very large claim may override the other claims. If it is proved afterwards that the claim does not exist, the whole position will be changed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Under the Bankruptcy Act as it now stands, I think such claims are allowed for the purposes of the meeting. The matter has all to go before the court for confirmation; there is nothing final about the meeting.
But what is there in the Act which makes it incumbent upon the man who sends a cablegram to follow it up with a sworn claim?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Under the general provisions of the Act in regard to every claim, proof must be submitted by affidavit and be open to the contestation of the trustee.
But this is an exception to the general rule.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, we make the exception only so far as the purposes of the meeting are concerned.
But after the vote has been taken it may be too late for redress.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That practice applies to all meetings of creditors in Ontario. The experience has not been that irregular or fraudulent claims are put in for the purposes of voting. I have attended many such meetings and have seen many telegraphic claims submitted. In this case everything is subject to inquiry and confirmation by the court.

Does my hon.
friend mean to say that in Ontario claims can be put in without being supported by affidavit, even for the purposes of such meeting?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That has been the practice for the last thirty or forty years. I fancy that the majority of proved claims at a meeting' under the Assignments and Preferences Act in Ontario are supported by nothing but letter, telegram, or individual representation. -
All I can say is that the people in Ontario are more honest than those in the other parts of the country.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: But that is only for the purposes of the meeting; the claims have to be verified and proved as required by the Act.

But it is not so stated, and it ought to be made perfectly clear. This cable or telegraphic communication is merely a temporary affair, and if when the claim is properly filed and sworn to it is found that it is wrong, there ought to be some proceedings to set aside what took place at that meeting or the decision there arrived at. I would ask the minister to allow this section to stand.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I have no objection.
Amendment stands.
Section stands.
On section 12-stay of proceedings pending consideration of proposal of composition, extension or scheme of arrangement.

As regards sub-clause 2 of this clause, I cannot see why the secured creditor's rights should be stayed by order of the court. If his right is secured by

law, why should he not proceed to collect his debt forthwith, because the trustee can do no more than the secured creditor himself, that is, sell the property that belongs to the estate and upon which security has been given, and turn the proceeds over to the secured creditor? It is only incurring further costs to have the proceedings stayed and to proceed afterwards along the same line.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do not think the
rights of secured creditors are prejudiced by this. The sub-clause reads:
Proceedings under this Act shall, subject to the rights of secured creditors to realize or otherwise deal with their securities stand stayed unless and until the court shall, on such terms as it may think just, otherwise order.
I think the court would take care of all rights under those circumstances.

What becomes of the claim of a creditor if a composition is made between the creditors and the debtor? Is the debtor relieved of any further liability? If a composition is executed, has a creditor any further claim for the balance of what is due to him, or is his claim discharged on account of the acceptance of a composition?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
If a composition or
agreement is made between debtor and creditors and confirmed by the court, such a composition would be upheld and the debtor released. But that is a matter of-agreement, and unless the proceeding laid down in the Act is complied with, no agreement would be made on the subject. In the main Act there is this further provision, section 13, sub-section 19:
Notwithstanding the acceptance and approval of a composition, extension or scheme, it shall not be binding on any creditor so far as regards a debt or liability from which, under the provisions of this Act, the debtor would not be discharged by an order of discharge in bankruptcy, unless the creditor assents,-
The creditor must agree.
-as, for the purposes solely of proceedings relating to a composition, extension or scheme he may, notwithstanding anything in this Act, so assent to such composition, extension or scheme.

As I understand the
matter, a debtor is in the hands of a majority of creditors at the meeting. If a majority of creditors want to accept an offer made by the debtor of a composition at so much on the dollar, and if that proposition is accepted, there is only the proceeding by which they go before the court and have the composition sanctioned by

the court. As I understand the matter, a majority of the creditors at the meeting can decide whether a debtor can be relieved of any other responsibility by paying five or ten or twenty cents on the dollar. If that is the way in which the law operates, I do not approve it; I think that is a bad principle; the claims of creditors who are in the minority are sacred and they should not be barred by a majority of the creditors at the meeting.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That was the law
which we adopted after a great deal of consideration and discussion in this House when we passed the Bankruptcy Act. I am not sure whether the provision says a majority or a two-thirds majority of the creditors-I am having that point looked up-but the principle is that where a man has been ordinarily honest and made full disclosure and handed over his assets, a majority or a two-thirds majority, I am not sure which, of the creditors may release him and bind the other creditors, provided that this is done in such a way as to receive the approval of the court.

If the creditors at the
meeting do not agree together, I understand that, under another of these amendments, a majority of the creditors have a right to override those who do not agree with them in order to secure, by a majority of the remaining creditors at a meeting held for the purpose, the acceptance of a proposition made by the debtor. There is danger in that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I am not proposing to
amend the Act as it now stands in that regard. Those clauses of the Act which were passed by Parliament as regards the discharge of debtors in bankruptcy proceedings, are still in the Act; and we do not propose to change them by the present Bill.
As the minister is aware, I have several amendments to the Act, and one of them deals with the question now before the committee. Might I ask the minister to allow this clause to stand?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I would be prepared
too discuss my hon. friend's amendments now.

I should like to discuss
them with the minister before they come before the committee. That would be much better for everyone concerned. I think my amendment is a little clearer than the one now before the committee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I should prefer not to
let any clauses stand if I can avoid that.

I have not this amendment with me just now.
Section stands.
On section 13-additional security to be given by trustee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The present section
provides that the registrar shall fix this security, and, of course, the registrar as a rule knows nothing about the estate. The proposed change, is to allow the creditors to fix the security, as set out in the proposed clause.

As the minister knows,
the security to be given by the' trustee consists of a general security in the form of a bond for $15,000 to be given to the state. When a trustee takes possession of an individual's estate, he has to give further security to the registrar. The proposed amendment reads:
If the creditors require the trustee to provide further security the trustee shall, within thirty days after the making of the receiving order or authorized assignment.

be obliged to give further security. Who are the creditors? Creditors at a meeting called for that purpose? A majority of the creditors or individual creditors? I think it would be clearer if we said: "If the creditors at a meeting called for that purpose," or "if a majority of the creditors at a meeting called for that purpose."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: To make that clear we could say "If the creditors present at any meeting."
Or "a majority of the creditors present."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That would mean a majority. The creditors could only act by a majority.
Would you not say "at a meeting called for that purpose?"

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I would not call a special meeting for that purpose. The more meetings of creditors, the more expense to the estate. They could discuss that at any meeting, I think, that was called. I do not want to encumber the Bill any more than is necessary with provisions as to meetings or applications to court or anything of that kind.
But there might be a hole-in-the-corner meeting.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is only one way of calling a meeting under the Act. I think if we said "If a majority of the creditors present at any meeting" it would be clear enough.
Duly called.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, duly called. I move that clause 13 be amended by striking out the words "the creditor" in line 17 of page 6 of the Bill and substituting therefor the following words "a majority of the creditors present at any meeting duly called." Amendment agreed to.

The last sentence in clause 13 does not seem to be quite what was intended. It says "the expense incident to the furnishing of such security may be charged by the trustee to the estate of the debtor." Why should the estate be ordered to pay that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We threshed that out when the Bill was before the House. The theory was this: The trustee has to pay for $15,000 of security out of his own pocket, which in the case of the ordinary estate ought to be sufficient. The creditors have the power to increase that amount, and if they do increase it, it is supposed to be for the general benefit of those who are participating in the estate, and the estate might therefore well bear the cost. We have left that clause exactly as it was in the Bill.
One difficulty is that the bankruptcy districts do not correspond with our judicial districts. In the province of Quebec, I understand there are only a few bankruptcy districts.
Only one.

Only one bankruptcy
judge.
That is what the Minister of Justice stated at the beginning of the session.
It would be more in accord with the principle of the Bill, I think, if there was an amendment providing for the creation of these districts.

This question of the districts came up at the beginning of the session, when the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) made some remarks upon it. I think it was well understood after the statement of the Minister of Justice that

there are nine bankruptcy districts in the Dominion of Canada, each province forming a district. I would suggest that each judge who has charge of a judicial district in the province of Quebec, composed of two or three counties, should have full authority under this law, as well as Mr. Justice Panneton residing in Montreal. I think that would be of advantage to all parties concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would not the hon. gentleman think that in view of the comparatively recent legislation which has divided the province of Quebec into four judicial districts, wherein there are resident judges, the case would be met by the province being so subdivided? Then you would have all the judges who are competent to sit in the different divisions resident in the respective divisions for the purposes of this Act. I understand that the Act provides that each province is a division, but that the Secretary of State may subdivide that division. If that were to be carried out, the question then would be, what would be the best subdivision to make in the province of Quebec, taking that province for example, and it occurred to me that perhaps a suitable subdivision would be to follow the subdivision which has created four districts wherein there are resident judges.

That would confine the subdivisions to the districts of Montreal, Quebec, Sherbrooke and Three Rivers. Under the new law the judges are supposed to reside in the district, and I respectfully submit that it would be a great deal more convenient to have the local judges, although they reside in Quebec, Montreal, Sherbrooke or Three Rivers, take charge of the administration of this law. Mr. Justice Panneton might administer the law in the district of Montreal, and the other judges in the districts outside the four principal districts under the new law. We have regular terms in our judicial district, and I believe the plan I have suggested would be more convenient to all parties concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggestion I make would only assimilate the insolvency business to all the other business. When the law, as I understand it, gets fully into operation, you will have no judges resident anywhere except in these four districts, and when it is completely carried out by the disappearance of judges who are attached to particular districts, there will be no judges attached to any particular

district. Therefore all the districts except the four mentioned will depend for their judicial service on judges coming from these four places. Why should it be more objectionable that judges coming from those four different places should deal with insolvency matters in those four different subdivisions of the province than that they should deal with all the business that has to be dealt with in the respective districts?

My objection is this. Take, for instance, the district of Kamouraska, the chief place in which is Riviere du Loup, in the county of Temiscouata. When the law is completely in force in the province of Quebec, when a judge comes to hear the civil cases, if he is not a judge appointed to hear- cases under the Bankruptcy Act, any bankruptcy cases there may be will have to be postponed till another term. This would delay matters unnecessarily, and I would suggest therefore that you give to all judges of the province of Quebec jurisdiction to hear cases under this law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No doubt the suggestion is worthy of consideration, but it seems to me that if it were adopted the whole principle ought to be changed and all judges of all the provinces ought to be given the same power: There is no special importance, in the case of Quebec, that I can see, to be attached to the suggestion, although it might possibly have been wiser to make it a function of any judge to hear these cases.

Why should it not be passible to vest in Ontario County Court judges, who sit in cities, the power to deal with these matters, instead of having it centralized in Toronto, where there has always been extreme congestion of litigation? It would mean a reduction in costs with a consequent saving to the estate. These judges are well qualified to deal with all these matters. County Court jurisdiction has now been extended in Ontario, so that these courts may deal with matters that formerly came within the jurisdiction of the High Court. It seems to me that this is a suggestion that might well be considered with a view to economy to all concerned.

The right hon. gentleman who is at the head of the Department of Justice (Mr. Doherty), has stated that in the province of Quebec there are four divisions wherein judges reside. This is
true. Recently two judicial appointments were made, one judge having been appointed for the district of Chicoutimi and another judge for the district of Beauce. Why should not these judges, who have special districts assigned to them, be given, besides the civil jurisdiction which they have, further jurisdiction under the Bankruptcy Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I intervened in this
matter only in so far as this particular question affecting Quebec is concerned. The Bill is in the hands of my colleague, the acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie).
I understand the situation in Quebec to be that, at the time the appointments to which the hon. gentleman refers were made, there was statutory provision that there must be a judge attached to each one of those districts and those judges were appointed and so attached. While I cannot now recall the details, I do understand that there has been passed, or, at all events, is in contemplation, according as vacancies occur in the judicial districts to which judges are specifically attached, provision that thereafter, in filling all places, judges shall be appointed simply as judges at large.
For the whole province, or for the four divisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, for the four sections. If I am correct in that regard, then the attaching of a judge for general purposes to a specific district is a purely transitory matter. I may say that in the appointments referred to these judges are attached to these particular districts for so long as the provincial law shall require that they be so attached; so that, if the provincial law should now be altered, they would cease to be attached to the particular districts and would become judges at large. That, of course, modifies the situation with regard to the administration of justice generally, and under those conditions it might be very inconvenient that a judge not particularly attached to a district should be charged with administering the Bankruptcy Act in that district. It was from that point of view that I thought that all purposes might be met if the judge from one of these four centres were appointed. It would be as easy for that particular one to go to outlying districts where there were bankruptcy matters to be considered as for some other judge to go to those districts.

I understand that Judge Panneton has been appointed for the whole

province of Quebec. Why should we not have a clause providing that a judge of the Superior Court may administer this law, so that whoever happens to be in the district at the time will have jurisdiction to do so?
What is the objection to haying judges of the various districts administer the law? What is the purpose in having only one judge?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not know why the Act was so drawn, but I remember that the committee that dealt with the Bill was strongly of the opinion that we should concentrate as far as possible and centralize for the purpose of uniformity, at all events, in the early stages of the administration of the Act. While this discussion may be useful, may I point out that we are dealing with the section in regard to security of trustees.
