Now, I am not familiar with the situation in the province of Quebec, but I know that the clause with reference to the jurisdiction of judges was under special consideration, and not only the committee, but the House was unanimous in the adoption of the section as it is drawn. The Act has been in force only eight months, and from the reports I have received, it is operating fairly well. If it were given another year or two we might be better able to judge then as to what amendments were necessary. In regard to judicial districts, there is power in the Act now to fix as many judicial districts as the Government may see fit to fix. The Governor in Council fixes the judicial districts, and if some bankruptcy districts should be set aside in the province of Quebec, the necessary legislative machinery is contained in the Act now to deal with the matter.

As a matter of fact, does this work take up the whole of the time of Mr. Justice Panneton? I have no objection to Mr. Justice Panneton, who is an eminent jurist and an able judge, but I thought it was hardly right to cast on his shoulders the whole administration of the Act for the province of Quebec. However, if it suits the litigants in my province, I have nothing more to say, but I cannot understand why the judge in each district is not vested with jurisdiction under this Act.

I may say, in answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux),-that Mr. Justice Panneton is not only able to attend to all bankruptcy business in Quebec but is also able to give time to the regular duties of the Superior Bench. The House will remember that the object of having one 
judge deal with bankruptcy matters to the exclusion of all others in each province was to give that judge an opportunity of familiarizing himself with the entire field of the law of bankruptcy. We thought that if one judge alone were to give his attention to this sole matter, in time he would become fairly familiar with the Act and in that way we thought the Act would work very much better than if we had seventeen or eighteen judges tinkering at it from time to time. At present there are nine judges, one for each province, who deal with the bankruptcy law of Canada, and if they keep on in that way, without molestation or interference by the Government, and without any tinkering with the Act, in time we shall have a fairly respectable body of jurisprudence which will be of some utility to people who are interested in bankruptcy matters. I for one would strongly oppose giving each judge of the High Court in the different provinces of Canada power to deal with bankruptcy questions. If we are to do that it is going to make this Act entirely nugatory and of no effect, and it will be only a question of a very short time when this Act will have to be repealed as the Acts of 1865 and 1874 were.

If such a contention should prevail, the Government would be bound to appoint a judge for the interpretation and enforcement of each law that is enacted by this Parliament, in order to get uniformity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This discussion on the division of districts is absolutely out of order on this clause. We have wandered away from the subject matter of the clause and I must ask the committee to return to it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 14-new trustee may be substituted.
What change has been made here?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The object of changing this is purely to clarify it. There has been some objection to the present clause which reads as follows:
A majority in number of the creditors who hold half or more in amount of the proved debts of twenty-five dollars or upwards may, at their discretion, at any meeting of creditors, substitute any other authorized trustee acting for or within the same bankruptcy district for the trustee named in the receiving order or to whom an authorized assignment has been made.
The new section is to qualify the meaning of that, and I think it is much clearer,

Creditors constituting a majority in number of those who have proved debts of twenty-five dollars or upwards and holding half or more in amount of the proved debts of twenty-five dollars or upwards may, at their discretion, etc.

In my opinion the
trustee, unless he is sick, or becomes dishonest or incapable of acting, should remain in that position until the matter is wound up.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, I do not agree with that.
. Mr. FORTIER: I do not see that this change is justified in any way. I do not think it is wise to change the trustee even if the majority of the creditors wish to do so. I see great objection to it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
My answer to that
would be that the creditors are the ones chiefly interested in the estate. Their interest is to get every dollar out of it if they can, and if, unfortunately, they have a trustee who is dilatory or careless, or is not an up-to-date business man, in the handling of the assets they may be very seriously prejudiced. The creditors are the ones who have the right to say as it is their interests he is looking after. Now it is provided that a majority of creditors representing a majority of the debts may change the trustee at their pleasure.
Without the intervention of the court?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, it says at any time. Mr. FORTIER: The matter is entirely disposed of by a majority of the creditors.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The creditors are
supreme in the matter.

Surely the court ought to have something to say in the matter of the change of a trustee? Supposing some of the creditors find after a trustee has been appointed that he has red hair and they do not like a man with red hair, can they out of pure caprice change this red-headed trustee for a man with black hair or no hair at all? Costs would be incurred by this change and the poor estate would have to bear them all in the end. It seems to me the judicial authority ought to interfere, and. some reason ought to be assigned why the change should be made. I would be perfectly ready to allow this to go through if some change were made whereby the court would have to become a party to it and authorize the change.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Oh, no. I think my hon. friend is contending for a principle that is absolutely wrong. The creditors
are to control and the trustee is trustee for the creditors.
Also for the debtor.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
More so for the
creditors. If the debtor is bankrupt or insolvent the trustee is trustee for the creditors. I think in the history of all bankruptcy legislation-in England, in the provinces undeT the provincial acts, and in the United States-the idea is to give the creditor absolute control and safeguard, so far as is possible, the rights of the debtor. Now all the trustees must be trustees who have been duly appointed and who have give given security. They are men of some standing in the first instance-they must be that before they are appointed. If the creditors say "We do not like our trustee A," why should they not have the right at any moment to put in B?

They are appointed by
court.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: None of them are.
They were originally.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, they are appointed by the Governor General in Council.
I mean for the estate.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, very often they
are appointed in the first instance by the debtor himself. He will pick a friend of his and make an assignment to his friend and the creditors may say "We don't want that man; we want another man." That has been the practice in all bankruptcy proceedings. Speaking of the province of Ontario, it has always been in our Assignment Act that the creditors shall have the selection or the removal of the trustee.

In cases where there is
only one trustee appointed in a particular district, is it possible to have another man appointed there who will be, you might say, competing with him?
Mr. GUTHRIE. There is no limitation at all to the number.

And any man who has
the qualifications and standing may get the position?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No. The manner in
which the Act has been applied, so far as regards the appointment of trustees is this. The administration of the Act is in the Department of the Secretary of State and I am not familiar with all the details of it-I have had nothing to do with it since the Act passed this House-but I believe

the requirement there is, first, that the man shall have some standing or qualifications for the position. The list has been confined, if not exclusively almost exclusively, to men who are chartered accountants, trust companies, or business men of large experience whose work has been in the nature of accounting or something of that kind. I do not think lawyers have been appointed in any instance.
No, it is against the law to have them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: But there is no limitation as to number at all.
Why does not the Civil Service Commission appoint them?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The Act provided they should be appointed by the Governor in Council.
More patronage.

I have not the section of the Act just before me, but as I remember it the creditors appoint the trustee, but with the authority or consent of the court 7 that is to say, the court takes some part in the appointment of this trustee. I may be wrong and I would like to he corrected if I am.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: If there is an application to the court on a receiving order, the court, of course, does issue the Order and the name of the trustee is in the order. But the experience of the Act jin the various provinces has been that only in one per cent of the cases has there been a receiving order; the rest have been the ordinary voluntary assignments and are ninety-nine cases out of a hundred. But if there is a receiving order, the court making the order nominates the trustee.
If the court does name the trustee under the receiving order-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The statute says that the court shall have regard to the wishes of the creditors in the selection of the trustee.

- If the court is a party to the appointment of the trustee, does not the minister think it is rather an anomaly that the trustee appointed by the court can be removed without the court being a party to his removal or the appointment of his successor?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, because I think
there will have to be another 9 p.m. receiving order, and in that case the court would again have to 
name the trustee. But the Act says that the court shall pay heed to the wishes of the creditors. I think it would be a fatal mistake to give any one except the creditors, who are chiefly interested, the right to say who shall or shall not be the trustee.
Under the present amendment the creditors, without giving any reason whatsoever, can remove the trustee and appoint another in his place.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
They can appoint
another authorized trustee.
I think we are making a mistake.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We made it a year ago after the gravest consideration.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-trustee may apply to court for directions:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
A mistake has been
made by the printer. In the last line but one there should be a comma after the word "of" and none after the word "justify."

Is this not rather an extraordinary provision? By this, whenever the trustee wishes to have any advice relating to any matter affecting the administration of the estate of the bankrupt, instead of applying to the attorney of the estate he must apply to the court. It is not in accordance with the usual practice.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It was not in the original Act. The reason for it is this: Trustees, particularly of large estates, are often met with a very difficult situation upon which there is a difference of opinion between the creditors

Let them go to their
attorneys.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: And this is giving the ordinary right to the trustee to go to the court for directions and protect himself. This is put in expressly at the request of the Association of Chartered Accountants. They say occasions have arisen when there is practically a dilemma, and their only safe course where they are under heavy bond is to ask for the instructions of the court.

But the duty of the court is to decide questions brought before it on motions or petitions. The proper parties who should be visited by the trustees are the attorneys of the estate; that is what they are there for. It seems to me we are cutting into the rights and prerog-

atives of the members of the bar by declaring that when trustees wish advice they shall go to the court.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, they may go. In the province of Ontario we have statutory provisions which enable trustees to go to the court to seek direction in difficult situations. They can go to their lawyers too, and they do. Very often exceedingly difficult problems arise in regard to the interpretation of wills and trust deeds, and the lawyers immediately ask the court for advice. That is the power that trustees ask for in bankruptcy proceedings.
Suppose the trustee goes to the lawyer and gets advice, and then goes to the court and gets different advice, what is he to do?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Go to another lawyer.

It seems to me rather
extraordinary that a private individual should go to the court to give him advice. The court is not there for that purpose.
He cannot get there without a lawyer, can he?
No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They have this provision in all the English speaking provinces. Have they not got it in the province of Quebec?

It strikes me that to safeguard the estate and prevent numerous applications for advice on the part of some timid trustee, it might be well to add that a trustee may at any time apply to the court for instructions when authorized by resolution of, say, a majority in amount of the creditors who have proven their debts against the estate. I would suggest that for the minister's consideration. In the event of an interminable number of applications the proceedings would be fairly expensive, and I think the trustee should not be given a free hand as in some cases he may abuse his trust.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am informed that the object of the section is to get around that difficulty of a majority of the creditors. Such a majority sometimes asks trustees to do what they should not do, and this section is to guard the trustees against that contingency.
They would suffer the loss themselves.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There would be no loss because the costs come out of the five per cent allowance.

But suppose a case
where creditors authorized the trustee to take a certain course of action in a sale of property, which results in a less amount than might have been received, then the creditors would suffer the loss and the trustee would not be responsible for the mistaken action he had taken. But if they have authority to authorize him to go to the court for certain purposes, then my suggestion would prevent numerous applications that might be made by some timid trustee who perhaps was friendly to the solicitor of the estate and was desirous of giving him a fairly large bill of costs.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It would not affect the solicitors because their costs are limited to a certain amount.
Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think this is in cases of difficulty where the creditors by a majority direct the trustee to take a certain line of action and he is doubtful as to its legality.
What are lawyers for?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Lawyers are sometimes doubtful themselves. That is the purpose of the Trustees' Relief Act, which enables an honest trustee to go to the court for advice and protection.

Let us take a concrete case. Suppose the trustee wishes to prosecute the bankrupt for some fraud, the only court before which the case can come is the court over which this judge in bankruptcy is presiding, and before these proceedings are taken we will say that the trustee has received advice from the judge of what he should do. The judge would therefore be acting as an adviser in the first place, and then he would be sitting as a judge to decide that his own advice Was good. That must appeal to the minister as being somewhat anomalous.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A prosecution for fraud is not under this Act, it is under the Criminal Code.

But in our province the judge inquires into all these matters as an examining magistrate and he sends the bankrupt up for trial. When the acting Solicitor General drafted this section he must have been doing it in his quality as Minister of Militia, because he rode roughshod over our laws. Certainly it is something that I strongly object to, and I would move that the clause be struck out.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: What clause?
The clause now under discussion, 16, adding subsection (d) to section 18 of the Bankruptcy Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The motion that a clause be struck out of a Bill is not in order, because it is an absolutely negative motion. There is a motion now before the committee that the clause do carry. The hon. member will, of course, have the right to vote against that motion.
We have done it with great success during the last three or four years. The rule must be one which has been more honoured in the breach than in the observance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A motion that a clause be struck from a Bill has never been put to the committee since I have occupied the chair. Motions have been made to amend clauses by striking out subclauses from clauses but no motions have been made to strike out entire clauses from Bills.

That is a distinction without a difference, in my mind.
Motion (Mr. Guthrie) carried on division: yeas, 33; nays, 22.
On section 18-permission limited to particular thing or class:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Section 20 deals with the powers exercisable by a trustee with permission of inspectors. The trustees themselves, or representatives of the trustee body, represented that there was sometimes a good deal of difficulty and inconvenience in obtaining the consent of inspectors to the particular acts enumerated in section 20. The section now provides that they may do certain things with the permission in writing of the inspectors, and it was represented that it would be much more convenient and more to the benefit of the estate if the provision for permission in writing was struck out. The English law from which this section was originally taken provides for the consent in writing. We refused to grant that amendment, but we thought it (would clarify subsection 2 if we repealed it and re-enacted it in the manner in which it appears in the Bill. The clause in the Act reads:
The permission given for the purposes of this section shall not he a general permission to do all or any of the above mentioned things but shall only be a permission to do any particular thing or things for which permission is sought in the specified case or cases.

The new section will be:
The permission given for the purposes of this section shall not be a general permission to do all or any of the above mentioned things but shall only be a permission to do the particular thing or things or olass of thing or things which the written permission specifies.
Under the original Act a separate permission had to be given for each of the particular acts enumerated in the paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h), (i), and (j). That was said to be very inconvenient. The proposal is that one single consent enumerating these will suffice for the various things desired, that is, that one consent or one permission may be given to do the particular thing or things or class of thing or things.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 21-removal of goods; bank deposits:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am told that the word "permission" is the one that should have been used in the first instance; there is "some technical distinction between "permission" and "consent." The latter, I believe has some ex post facto operation that the word "permission" does not have. The word in the English Act is "permission."
What is the original section?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It reads:
No property of an estate of a bankrupt or of an authorized assignor shall be removed out of the province where such property was at the date when any receiving order or authorized assignment was made, without the consent in writing of the inspectors-
It will now read "permission in writing."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 22-trustee	carrying on
business of debtor may apply to court for sale of property by tender if creditors refuse or neglect to repay advances.
Who controls this expenditure by the trustees?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The creditors do, and the creditors must authorize the trustee to do any acts contemplated in section 27 of the present Act or in the proposed amendment. The trouble occurs, particularly in large estates where heavy expenditures are required, and where the trustee is directed, we will say, to continue the business of a creditor under section 27. In doing so, he incurs obligations, and in many cases trustees have themselves made considerable advances. The difficulty then

is to get the money back. This section is not new to our law; these provisions are taken from the clauses in our Winding-up Act which makes similar provisions; but for some reason or another they were omitted when the Bankruptcy Act was first passed. This is to indemnify the trustee in respect of money advanced by him or for obligations which he has assumed for the benefit of the estate.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	For money advanced under instructions of the creditors only?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That is all,
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Does the minister not think that it would be advisable to have a certain delay of, say three or four months, before a trustee could sell a property, so as to give the creditors time to reimburse the trustee for certain expenses such as city taxes and so on? In certain cases, valuable property could pass into the hands of a trustee and a creditor would lose all recourse as the property would be sold to reimburse the trustee. A business might be so conducted by the trustee that a creditor might not see what was going on, and the creditor might be brought slowly to bankruptcy in his own business. The minister should see that all the rights of creditors are very carefully safeguarded in this matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: So far as my knowledge goes, this is a clause that has never opened the door to any abuse under the Winding-Up Act, but it takes a considerable time before a trustee can realize under the provisions of this clause. In the first place, if he wants his money back, he has to make a ten days' demand; in the second place, he has to make an application to the court; and in the third place, the estate will have to be advertised for thirty days. Then tenders are opened and a decision is come to. There would be two or three months' delay in any event, and I do not think there could be any hardship on the part of creditors.

I notice that we are
taking precautions to safeguard the rights of trustees. Take the case where a bank has made advances to a trustee, that is, in his quality of trustee. Does the minister not think that the bank or any person who makes such advance or advances, should be put in the same position as the trustee?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think the bank will
take care of itself.

In paragraph (d), there is this provision:
After such notice to the debtor and the creditors as to it may seem proper, permit the trustee

, And so forth. Many of those creditors may be out of the jurisdiction of the court. There should be some definite statutory provision that, in a clause as drastic as this, notice should be given which might reach such creditors through the mail or ultimately reach them by personal service, preferably through the mails, because that would be cheaper. Advertising in the Gazette does not reach the ordinary creditor. Many creditors may be in different parts of the province, and an advertisement in a Toronto paper might not reach creditors in other parts of Ontario. The provision might be extended a little in order to protect the creditors.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That difficulty must
have been present in the minds of the draftsmen of the section in the Winding-up Act, because it * leaves the matter entirely to the judgment and discretion of the court-such as to the court may seem proper-and I think the court would be careful to protect the rights- of creditors in the way of notice.
I do not think it would.

I do not know how
these laws concerning liquidation work in the other provinces, but I know how they work in my province. The net result of most liquidations is that the liquidator has a certain amount of costs, very high as a rule; the two lawyers have also costs, and the creditors, when they look at the dividends, have nothing at all. That is the common experience throughout my province. This clause simply says that if the costs or expenses incurred by the liquidator during the liquidation are so high that nobody wishes to pay them, the liquidator can take over the property and pay himself. It is a very dangerous law. These liquidators are practically under no observation. Who watches them? The creditors, as a rule, especially When the company in liquidation is a company of importance, are business men who have to attend to their businesses, and the liquidators are left to attend to the winding-up of the business. If the liquidators pile on the costs and expenditures, they can take advantage of this clause and take over the property. I do not know how the law works in the other provinces; but in my province it does not work in a very

satisfactory manner, and by this clause we are giving to the liquidators more power than they have already and most business people think that they have too much already.
The situation in Ontario is worse.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There is no change in
this section except that we have struck out the words "to any other person" in the second line of the old section. The old section read, "Where a person engaged in any trade or business makes an assignment to any other person." These words were not necessary, and it was said by one judge that they might exclude a trust company, that the definition of the word "person" as it was in the original Act would not be broad enough to include a trust company, and he suggested that the words "to any other person" be struck out. They are not necessary, and I agree that they should come out. It has been deemed proper to reprint the whole section so that a person reading the new section would not have to have two statutes before him to see what was meant.

Notwithstanding the
small change that has been made, I would like to call attention to the effect of this section, and no doubt the effect of the section as it was originally passed. Starting at line 21 the section reads "the assignment of book debts shall be void"-meaning a general assignment, as is plain from the closing paragraph of the section; then going down to line 25 "unless there has been compliance with the provisions of any statute which now is or hereafter may be in force in the province wherein such person resides or is engaged in said trade or business as to registration, notice and publication of such assignments."
I understand that in the province of Quebec, and perhaps in the majority of the provinces of Canada, there are statutory provisions which can be followed as to registration, notice and publication, and that therefore the lender, be he banker or any other man with capital, can protect himself under the provisions of these statutes; but in the province of Ontario, if I am right, there is no provision of that kind, and a general assignment of book debts cannot be registered under any provincial statute; so that the effect of this clause in that province is that a general assignment of book debts is void. That perhaps is a

good condition, or it may perhaps be a poor one. The effect, I think, will be that banking credits will be restricted to borrowers because of the insecurity offered to the bank in the case of an assignment. I ask leave to read a portion of a letter I have received from a well-known chartered accountant in Toronto, whose experience in these matters is perhaps as wide as that of anybody else in the Dominion. After discussing the clause, he says:
To my mind it will be exceedingly unfortunate if the section should be continued in this form, particularly in the present uncertain times when credit is difficult enough to obtain under any circumstances and many businesses are embarrassed with deflation. If the section be so continued it will simply mean that credit to wholesale grocers, boot and shoe men, dry goods and other jobbers and distributors will be limited to greater or lesser extent. The idea has seemed to prevail that it is the banks who are moving to have the section deleted, but I do not understand that that is the case, for the attitude which the banks take is that they are quite prepared to lend money when it is safe to do so and they can get proper security. If they cannot get security, then they cannot make the loans. It will, therefore, mean that the responsibility will rest upon the Government, of passing legislation which has the effect of impairing the liability of such concerns to get necessary credit. In this view it does seem to me that the condition of affairs should not be looked at from a narrow standpoint, but I feel that in the general interests of the community the section should either be deleted or amended so that assignments of accounts can be given as the basis -of banking accommodation.
I am not here to speak on behalf of the banks. I am not interested in any bank to the extent of a single halfpenny. I run a rival institution to a bank, an institution that does not deal in this class of thing at all, but I have some knowledge of this gentleman, I know his experience, and I thought the least I could do was to let his views be known to the committee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
When this clause as framed in the original Act was before'the Special Committee, I doubt if any other clause received the same amount of attention and discussion. The question was as to the right of banks to take secret liens unknown to other creditors. It was contended before that committee, in the first place, that section 88 of the Bank Act should not be allowed to prevail in the case of bankruptcy. Section 88 of the Bank Act is the section which permits banks to take warehouse receipts, which are a form of secret security unknown to the general trading public. In the event of subsequent assignment or bankruptcy it very often happens that under section 88,

the bank under its warehouse or secret lien gets practically the whole estate.
The next question argued at length before the committee was the question of general assignment of book debts, that is, an assignment of all present and future book debts. It became an established practice in commercial life to recognize the validity of such commercial assignments. Time after time in my own experience in the province of Ontario, where insolvency proceedings took place, it would be found that some selected creditor had secretly obtained an assignment of book debts, and it was held under the Ontario law as it then existed that book debts did not pass to the assignee under the general assignment. This one creditor was preferred to all the others, and it very often happened that the book debts were the most valuable part of the estate.
The committee heard representatives of the Bankers' Association on this clause, of the Wholesale and Retail Merchants' Associations, and of other associations. Upon this particular clause the committee was unanimous, and I think the House of Commons was also unanimous when the question came before it. We were supposed to draft and enact a clause which would prevent persons, including banks, from taking a secret assignment of book debts present and future, but it was argued that in one or two provinces of Canada such assignments had been recognized by the statutes of the province, which provided that such assignments were valid if they were registered, if notice thereof was given to the public. The committee thought that that was a reasonable provision. Consequently, in the section we drew in the Bankruptcy Act we provided that if the person seeking to have an assignment of present and future book debts complied with the provincial requirements as to registration and notice, that would be sufficient in that province to protect the public and the transaction should be held to be valid, but throughout the rest of Canada where there was no such provision for registration and notice, such general assignment of book debts should not be permitted to prevail against the trustee in bankruptcy. That was the unanimous view of the committee at that time. 1 That is what we thought we had done when we enacted the section under consideration now. Several representatives of the Bankers' Association have interviewed me recently in regard to this clause. They complain that the clause is somewhat doubtful, and several very elaborate legal
opinions have been submitted to me by very eminent counsel, but the most that 1 could gather from the various opinions was that there might be an element of doubt as to the bank's right to take a general assignment of book debts. I said that if there was doubt about the matter, the section should clear it up, and that plain and definite language should be employed if the language at present were at all doubtful. I think that the opinion of the House to-day would be as it was two years ago, that such assignments should not be permitted. However, as the Act has only had eight months of operation, and as there has yet been no judicial decision upon the section as it stands, a case not yet having arisen before the courts, I thought it would be just as well to allow the section to stand in order to see what could and could not be done under it. I am satisfied that our intention, by the language we used, was to prevent banks or other persons from taking general assignments of book debts which were in the nature of secret securities.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Is an assignment of a debt or claim on a mortgage to a third party, good if made thirty days before a man becomes insolvent, or does the debt or claim pass to the assignee? In the province of Quebec there is a law which provides that a transfer is good if made in good faith thirty days before a man becomes insolvent. As I understand this section that provincial law will be overridden. What I want to know is whether a transfer of a claim or mortgage made thirty days previous to bankruptcy in the province of Quebec will be good?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not know that I was able closely to follow my hon. friend, but I think he has asked a question which involves very difficult sections of our Bankruptcy Act, sections 29, 30, 31 and 32, in regard to preference and preferential payments. The section under consideration now involves only the single question of assignments of book debts, and there is no limitation of thirty days under that section. The question which my hon. friend asked, if I understood him rightly, does not arise under this section. I think section 29 of the Bankruptcy Act would apply to his question. However, the question is one that requires a good deal of legal consideration, and if the hon. gentleman would ask my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), that hon.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
member could tell him, as readily as I could, the law on the point.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: I think the minister should attempt to answer the question now. According to this section, a transfer of book debts in Quebec, notwithstanding the provincial law, will not be good, even though it is made thirty days before bankruptcy.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I thought you said mortgage.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	Well, the law
would apply to that too. Under the law of Quebec any transfer of goods, money, etc., made thirty days before bankruptcy, holds good. Will that law be respected under this paragraph?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This paragraph will
have no application whatever to that; it deals only with general assignment of book debts. This section does not affect the assignment of specific debts. In Quebec or Ontario you can still make an assignment to a bank or any other person of a specific book debt, which is perfectly good; this refers only to general assignments of present and future book debts.

In Quebec we have certain provisions in the code of civil procedure regulating what we call the abandonment of property; that is, a debtor abandons the whole of his property to his creditors. Suppose such an abandonment takes place under the provisions of the provincial code of civil procedure, and another creditor takes proceedings under this law; in what position would the debtor be? Does this federal law give to the liquidator who might be appointed under it the right to put aside altogether the provincial law and disregard the code of civil procedure of the province? I know my hon. friend the Solicitor General is not as familiar with our civil law as his neighbour the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), and if he cannot answer this question perhaps the right hon. gentleman will do so. We shall be very grateful to him if he does. This clause involves an important question. This new bankruptcy law contains many sections that are in absolute opposition to our civil laws of Quebec. There has been a principle of constitutional procedure in Canada which has always been respect-
10 p.m. ed, and that is that, as regards civil rights, the provinces are the paramount authority. We have special provisions concerning civil rights, and

if I understand this clause rightly provincial legislation will be set aside. Have we, as a Federal Parliament, without changing our constitution, the right to pass such a law? I believe we have not.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There may be some
doulbt upon the question, but I thought that we cleared up all doubts when the Act was originally before the House. My hon. friend knows that among the subjects that come within the special jurisdiction of this Parliament un ler the British North America Act are the subjects of bankruptcy and insolvency, and I think in the year 1874, we passed an Insolvency Act applicable to the whole Dominion. The constitutionality of that Act was challenged in the courts and cases went to the Privy Council, where it was held that the Act was unconstitutional. That Act was repealed and for many years in Canada we had not any act passed by this Parliament in respect of bankruptcy and insolvency. During the interval many of the provinces passed Acts which were tantamount to insolvent legislation. We in the province of Ontario had an Act respecting assignments and preferences by insolvent persons. There were other Acts in other provinces to the same effect, and the Privy Council held, in respect of these Acts-because there were appeal? in respect of them -that whereas the Dominion Government had not occupied the field of legislation pertaining to bankruptcy and insolvency, the provincial legislation was good in the absence of Dominion legislation upon the same subject; but at the moment the Dom inion Parliament should occupy that field, and should pass an Act in respect of bankruptcy and insolvency, provincial legislation to that effect would be set aside. Now my contention, and I believe it is properly founded, is that we have in the present bankruptcy law occupied that particular field of legislation, and that all provincial legislation which seeks to contravene or oppose the Dominion legislation would be ultra vires of the province that passed it. I do not know of the Act referred to by my hon. friend whereby a debtor may abandon all his property to his creditors. I would only say, on general principles, that if the debtor so doing were, as a matter of fact, in insolvent circumstances at the time, that Act would be an Act of bankruptcy under our present law. If the debtor at the time of the abandonment, were a solvent person I do not think it would be considered an Act of bankruptcy. Generally speaking, I sup-

pose that abandonment, if it were an abandonment of all his property, would be equivalent to the old form of general abandonment under the Ontario Act, and that always was looked upon as an Act of insolvency in that province.

The Acting Solicitor
General is perfectly right when he states that the British North America Act gives to the Federal Government jurisdiction concerning bankruptcy and insolvency, hut does not my hon. friend believe that this competency of the Federal Government extends to the procedure, or to the forms of law to be followed, whenever a person is insolvent or bankrupt, and does not go so far as to give to Parliament the authority to put aside the rights-the civil rights or the rights of ownership-which are altogether under provincial jurisdiction? For instance, in the province of Quebec we have certain provisions of our civil law concerning mortgages. Does my hon. friend contend that this clause of the British North America Act concerning bankruptcy and insolvency would give to this Parliament jurisdiction to set aside the special provisions of our legislature concerning mortgages or rights of property within our province? This Parliament, I think, has a perfect right to pass whatever law it deems fit to provide the means, or the method, or the mode, by which a person may be declared insolvent or bankrupt and by which that person's property may be distributed among his creditors, but I do not think that this Parliament could go beyond that and put aside the rights of property, or the civil rights, which are altogether invested in the provincial legislatures. I claim that in this Act there are several clauses which do so. As far as those clauses are concerned, is this law constitutional? I have great respect for my hon. friend's legal talent and knowledge, but I doubt very much whether his interpretation of the British North America Act is right when he extends it to such a point that the Federal Parliament would have a right to attack civil rights which are altogether left to the provincial legislature.

Regarding what the
minister in charge of the Bill said respecting section 23, any one in practice knows that we frequently are confronted with an assignment of these unregistered book debts. The principle of it is just as the minister has said-vicious. They may be the chief asset of the estate. If it were
an assignment of chattel property that requires, under the law of Ontario, to be registered. I cannot speak for any other province than the province of Ontario, and I do know that it is working a hardship there that we have no such requirement as the registration of these assignments. I think it would be a very good thing if, in this Act, we made it the law that such assignments are void unless they comply with the Act, if there be such an Act, but if there be no Act that they are absolutely void. That will compel our province to pass an Act stating what should be the requirement. I would like to move an amendment to that effect that in line 30, after the word " assignment " the following words be added:

and if there be no such statute as to registration, notice and publication of such assignment, then such assignment shall be void.
That will make it perfectly clear. To-day, under that section, you could have a very nice lawsuit in the province of Ontario as to whether or not an assignment of book debts-where there is no requirement as to notice and registration-is, after the passing of this Act good or bad. Why put out legislation like that? We ought to make it specific one way or the other, and clearly it is to the interest of the public to have no more secret assignments; let them all be public.
Would the hon. gentleman include assignments to banks? I do not think it is fair to bring up in connection with this legislation what is in reality an amendment to the Bank Act.
I am not talking about the Bank Act.
Well in the case of manufacturing concerns everybody knows very well there is a blanket assignment to the banks when they are borrowing thousands of dollars.
This deals with book debts.
Well book debts are also included in an assignment to a bank.
An assignment of book debts will not put them under this legislation. [DOT]
I think an assignment covers books debts.

Is it not rather dangerous to enter upon legislation of this kind offhand without giving the matter suffi-

cient consideration? The assignment of a book debt is recognized in common law. It is property and if it is absolutely assigned in writing and notice given to the man from whom the debt is due that completes the transfer of property to the assignee That is, if a man owes me a debt and I assign it to another man he notifies the debtor that the debt is due to him instead of to me. We put that assignment on record under our General Registration Act.
Where?
In our province we would put it in the registry of deeds the same as a bill of sale.

I 'know of no such provision in Ontario and that is the difficulty we are up against. I am only now speaking on behalf of Ontario, and we have no such provision as that. We have a provision in the Bill of Sales Act and the Chattel Mortgages Act requiring within ten days that the transaction be registered; also in the case of liens, sales of wagons and things like that where there is a lien held upon the property; but the public to-day may be entirely misled by a man's status and the fact be that everything in the way of book debts has been already assigned to some creditor, a bank or somebody else. I have often acted in a case where such an assignment has been made to one creditor making him, as the minister said, preferred to everybody. If that be the case make it public. Of course I am speaking only of Ontario. We are deficient in that respect, and this would force the province, at the request of the financial institutions, to pass an Act that would enable those transactions to be perfectly good upon complying with its terms.

I have not given any definite opinion about it at all. Under the old common law a debt or chose in action was not assignable, but an English statute -which is as old as the hills and is now regarded practically as common law- altered that condition of affairs. That law is in force in Canada to-day. But it strikes me that if the assignment is properly made and is put on record it is perfectly valid.
That is the point. We have no place for registration.
If that is not the law, 1 would like to know what the law is.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is not the question raised in this section.
In Ontario an assignment, coupled with notice, completes the transfer of the debt. There is no requisite of registration. Indeed, there is no place I know of where it can be recorded.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A specific book debt can be assigned now to a bank or anybody else. This section does not interfere with but protects that. But let me make this suggestion. I understand there is some litigation on this section now. A representative of the Bankers' Association asked me if we would let the question stand and take what action might be deemed advisable next session in the light of the judicial decision on that litigation. Therefore I think it will be better to leave the section as it it, striking out the words "any person" as I moved in the first instance.
I do not know how we can legislate along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Port Arthur because I do not think we have any jurisdiction unless the person becomes insolvent.
I am only speaking of general, not special debts.

It seems to me rather important that the point raised by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) should not pass without some comment in that it creates a doubt as to the authority of Parliament to legislate in this regard. The cases referred to by the Solicitor General which went to the Privy Council turned beyond a shadow of doubt on the question whether the power of the Dominion was paramount over that of the provinces, and it was clearly determined that the Dominion law when once enacted took the place of any provincial law. In those very cases the point was brought up that such legislation by the Dominion would constitute interference with property and civil rights which the British North America Act places under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but it was held by the Privy Council that in view of the wording of the other subsection bankruptcy and insolvency came under the jurisdiction of the Dominion, which dispossessed the power of the provinces in so far as the Dominion might go. I am sorry that I cannot recall the names of those cases. It is natural that the provinces should be jealous of any interference with their laws, but the demand for this bankruptcy legislation has come from the provinces themselves, in order that it may be uniform, as on account of the great increase in commercial transactions

between the provinces it was thought unfair to the commercial community that they should be left in doubt as to the law. By having a uniform bankruptcy law throughout the Dominion a merchant in Winnipeg, for instance, selling to another merchant in Quebec would know what his rights were against his debtor without having to inquire how the provincial law affected him. It seems to me all-important that we should not throw any doubt upon a law demanded for the whole Dominion which will make transactions of sale and barter between the provinces much more easy and convenient, especially as we have a declaration by the highest court in the Empire that the Dominion law is paramount in this respect.

As my hon. friend from Parkdale has just said, there are two classes of people in Canada who represent two opinions; the first class think that our Federal Parliament has an authority superior in all domains to the provincial legislatures, and the second class think that the provincial legislatures are just as powerful and have exactly the same potency of jurisdiction within their own limits as the Federal Parliament itself. There is another class of opinion among the legal men of this country; they wish to have uniformity in all legislation. The hon. member for Park-dale said that it would be a very good thing if a merchant in Manitoba when dealing with another merchant in Quebec knew that the law in the latter province was the same as that which existed in his own province. I do not wish to discuss whether this doctrine is good or bad, but I desire to say that in the province of Quebec the vast majority of the people and also the vast majority of members of the legal profession, although they wish to have as complete and perfect a set of Canadian laws as possible, also wish to see respected to the fullest extent the rights of the provincial legislatures under the British North America Act. And if there is one thing which not only the legal men of the province of Quebec but also the population of that province desire it is that the beautiful set of civil laws which have come to us from France, laws which were borrowed by France from Rome -and as we all know Mr. Chairman, the Romans were the greatest legislators in the world's history; they seem to have been natural lawyers-laws which were brought over by the first French pioneers, should remain to them unimpaired. As everybody knows those laws were codified later by Napoleon the First and are now
embodied in our civil code. The province of Quebec is just as proud of her civil code as of any other monument in her possession, and I think the provincial government will always do its very best to preserve intact those civil laws. As one of the representatives of the province of Quebec, and also as a lawyer from that province having some knowledge of her civil laws, I say it would be a great danger to our province if this Parliament was allowed to put aside the provisions of the British North America Act and to override our provincial laws concerning property rights. The member for Parkdale has quoted a decision of the Privy Council, the highest judicial authority in the Empire. But in many of the decisions of that body there is indicated a very strong tendency to strengthen the hands of the federal authority and to weaken those of the provincial authority. As has been stated by the member for Parkdale as well as by the Acting Solicitor General, it is true that bankruptcy and insolvency are subjects within the jurisdiction of the federal authority, but under no pretext or excuse whatsoever can the Federal Parliament put aside the rights of the Provincial Legislature with regard to civil rights and property. This law of bankruptcy is a great danger to the province of Quebec because it contains several clauses setting aside our civil law. The Minister of Justice is a learned jurist. He has been an ornament to the Quebec Bench; he upheld while on the bench those old civil laws of Quebec which he admires and loves, I am sure, as much as every other Quebec man does. The right hon. gentleman should use his influence with his colleague the Acting Solicitor General to see that none of the laws passed by this Parliament shall put aside the civil law of Quebec or of any other province and that due respect shall be given to the old principles guiding legislation by the Federal Parliament and the Provincial Legislature.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I cannot very well
agree to the amendment, for the reasons which I have stated. There are some cases now pending in the courts with regard to this section, and unless it is the very strong desire of the mover of the amendment and of the committee that it be changed, I should like the section to have operation until next session so that we may see what the courts have to say about it.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	Before passing
such an amendment a notification should be sent to the provinces, because in some of

the provinces there is no office where such registration could he made.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That has been done.
Amendment (Mr. Keefer) negatived, and section agreed to.
On section 25-when misrepresentation or fraud a defence for contributory to insolvent incorporation:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That omission was
purely accidental. It is in the Winding-up Act and it should have been in the Bankruptcy Act.

I do not quite see the force of this amendment. I think the rule is that any defence which is good against the assignor should be good against the assignee. If the man who made the assignment could not by reason of fraud succeed in getting this amount from the contributory, why is the right to that defence to disappear simply because there is an assignment? I would like to know upon what principle this right is being taken away?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well, the provision was designed in order to do away with what would be the ordinary rule to which my hon. friend has referred. It has been on our statute book for a long time. It applies only, of course, to the case of corporations. The experience was that when a corporation got into financial difficulties, made an assignment or got into bankruptcy, it was very difficult to get in the unpaid calls on stock and the defence of fraud became very common. The defence of fraud is still permitted, provided that action to set aside the subscription is instituted before the assignment.

But suppose the fraud
does not come to the attention of the plaintiff until after the assignment, is the defence taken away by this amendment?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Certainly that is most
unjust.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It has been a long time our law.
Then it has been unjust a long time.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It remedied a very
great wrong, a gross abuse which had grown up. The experience was that in every case where a corporation went into insolvency, people who had not paid up their stock wanted to escape payment or to delay it. The defence of fraud and mis-

representation became common. To remedy that state of things, not only here, but in Great Britain, this clause was framed, and it has been for many years in our Winding-Up Act. I have never heard of any exception being taken to it.

Supposing we say in
this case that this defence could not be set up if the debtor or the stock subscriber should set up that plea, say over six months after the fraud had been committed or the knowledge of such fraud had come to him. Supposing he had never heard about that fraud before, would he be denied altogether the right of setting up fraud or misrepresentation in the case?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The same provision
exists in the Winding-up Act.

Even if it exists in one law, if the principle is unfair, why should we extend it throughout our legislation? After all, what do the liquidators represent? The liquidators in a way represent all the rights that a corporation may have. In one way, a liquidator might be what we might call the collector or representative of all the creditors, and he is nothing more. In the case of a corporation he represents simply the corporation itself. If I had a good defence to set up against a corporation, why should I not be permitted to set up that defence against the liquidator who represents nothing but the corporation?

The minister ought to
consider very carefully the objections to this clause. Supposing, after all the books, papers and documents of a company come into the hands of a liquidator, the subscriber finds the grossest kind of fraud; surely he ought to be able to set that up when he is sued for the balance due on his stock.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This provision should certainly come out of the Winding-up Act, if my hon. friend's contention is good.
Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof. Two wrongs do not make a right, and they never did.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It is quite immaterial to me what the committee does with this clause, but it has stood the test of time in the Winding-up Act without objection. So far as I am aware, no objection has been raised to it in this House for twenty years. Now we are trying to make the law uniform, so that it will apply under the

Bankruptcy Act just as it does under the Winding-up Act.

The minister must
remember that we are going to have thousands and thousands of cases under this legislation which is of general application throughout Canada from coast to coast, whereas, it is only here and there and on rare occasions that any proceedings are taken under the Winding-up Act. Even if this provision were in the Winding-up Act, we would come up against it only once in a while; whereas now, under this general law, we will come up against this provision ten times every day. If promoters of some kind of a company go around the country gathering up subscriptions and getting people to subscribe to the stock under fraudulent circumstances, and they deceive a man into signing his name to a subscription list or giving a note for a share or something like that, and they immediately make an assignment just for the purpose of getting clear under this provision, is it not too bad that they should be able to succeed by simply putting the whole thing under the Insolvency Act and thus shutting the man's mouth? He cannot say a word; he has to pay out his hard cash absolutely for nothing, and he is robbed. We are passing legislation which will help those who are unfair to him. If a transaction is right, above board proper and honest, the man who starts to collect a debt has nothing to fear if the debtor is worth it; but it is too bad that the debtor should be deprived of a good and sound defence if the transaction is not a proper one, simply because there is a transmission or passing over of a claim from one concern to another. We should be very careful abbut a provision of this kind.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We are taking great care in the matter by making the two Acts uniform. At the present time the Winding-up Act is in force, and corporations may be wound up under that Act in which this same provision appears. Corporations may be wound up under the Bankruptcy Act, but only by leave of the court. If the court gives leave to have them wound up under the Bankruptcy Act, surely the same general provision as regards unpaid stocks should prevail in both Acts. I am told that the experience under the old system was very bad. The rights of creditors were greatly prejudiced by fictitious defences, defences put in to gain time; delays were occasioned, and in order to remedy that improper and unfair condition to creditors,
to get rid of those delays, this provision was inserted in the Winding-up Act.

The minister can see
how unjust this provision would be in certain cases. The courts are organized for the purpose of deciding these questions as between the parties.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think it would be open to my hon. friend to say if application is made to the court to wind up a corporation under the Bankruptcy Act: "There is a more favourable provision under the Winding-up Act. Therefore, I want to get under the Winding-up Act, because under the Bankruptcy Act there is not this provision." Or, if he were acting for some holder of unpaid stock, he might take the reverse position and say:	"We want to
come under the Bankruptcy Act, because it allows defences which are not allowed under the Winding-up Act," and the court would decide.

Assuming, for the sake of argument, that the same provision appears in the Winding-up Act, that is no reason why we should perpetuate it in this new Act which we are bringing into life. We will deal with the provision in the other Act in due course now that we know of it; but at present, while we have this provision formally before us, we ought not to enact it into legislation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not want to strike it out. I am not the one who made the suggestion.
Let the clause stand.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We will have to have a vote on it. I do not know that I can elaborate the matter any further; but as my hon. friend apparently wants to divide the committee on this clause, we had better have a little larger committee than we have at the present moment.
I know my hon. friend has more members behind him than I have, and so he will be able to carry the clause.	r

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Carried on division?
Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to, on division.
On section 26-adjustment of rights of contributories.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This is the adjustment of the rights of contributories. The old section provides:
The court shall, on the application of any contributary, adjust the rights of the contribu-

tories among themselves without the intervention of the trustee and without expense to the estate.
The section in this Bill provides:
The court may, on the application of any contributory, adjust the rights of the contributories among themselves, and,-
What follows is new-
-for the purpose of facilitating such adjustment may direct the trustee to interevene-
The other section was "without the intervention of the trustee."
-carry the proceedings, employ legal or other assistance and make such investigations, do such acts, and furnish such information as to the court may seem necessary or advisable.
The proposed amendment is consequential upon this one, and provides that the court may allow remuneration and expenses to the trustee from the contributories who are contestants, but not from the estate. The obj'ect of the two sections is that where disputes arise as between contributories the trustee may intervene, seek the judgment of the court, and have the rights of the contributories as between themselves settled, but without expense to the estate.

It seems to be a sort of jug-handled arrangement. Why is it that the Acting Solicitor General is so anxious about the rights of the estate and trustee, and seems to ignore altogether the rights of others? If it is necessary to have litigation between the contributories and the estate through the trustee, why should the costs not be ordered to be paid to the contributories?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend speaks about my being anxious about the rights of the estate and the trustee, and not about the rights of others. Now the courts cannot act in this case unless the contributories themselves call upon them to do so, and the trustee cannot go to the court until the contributory has applied. This is to settle disputes as between themselves without expense to the estate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 27-court may allow remuneration, expenses and costs as between contributories:
Suppose the court refuses in this case to intervene. How will things be adjusted?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They will have to have recourse to the ordinary remedies according to the law of the land, and expensive litigation will ensue.
If that is the case, why have these other sections at all? Why bother with them?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This is designed for a speedy and inexpensive settlement of disputes.	*

Security is usually provided by some person not a resident within the province or country. I do not see why the court should insist upon the contributories giving security if they are resident in the province.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The contributories cannot be forced to come to court under this. They must be the parties themselves to go to court, and if they do, they come under the provisions of this section. If they do not desire to go to court, they need not. They can have recourse to the ordinary remedies and fight it out. There is nothing compulsory about this. It is only a method to afford quick and cheap relief.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section; 28-right of creditor to dividend:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Subsection 3 of section 37 reads:
Any creditor who has not proved his debt' before the declaration of any dividend or dividends shall be entitled-
We propose to add there the words "upon proof of such debt."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 29-notice that if claim not proved within 30 days dividend or final dividend will be made:

How can this section be
reconciled with the preceding one? The preceding one says they can always obtain payment providing they prove their claim, whereas this section provides that unless the creditor's claim is proved within a certain time, the trustee may proceed to make a dividend without regard to his claim.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
With regard to dividends and the distribution of dividends, there are no less than nine sections, and the one I just read is only one showing what rights the creditor has in respect to making proof of bis claim. This is to hurry up distribution. In practice it has been found that creditors withheld proof of their claim until after notice of the final dividend, and this delayed the winding up of the estate to the great prejudice of every one concerned. This changes the present law to this effect, that the trustee

may at any time after the first meeting of creditors-he does not have to wait until after the final notice-give notice hy registered mail to every person of whose claim to be a creditor with a provable debt he has notice or knowledge.

Under the first clause,
if there is no such notice sent, the creditor may be paid even after the dividend list has been prepared, hut under this clause the creditor has to prove his debt within thirty days after the mailing of the notice, or he will have no further claim.

I do not think the section is very clear about thirty days being allowed. It might be only one day and the provision might be abused. At line 45 it is provided that:
If such person does not prove his debt within a time limited by the notice (which shall be within 30 days after the mailing' of the notice) the trustee will proceed to make a dividend or final dividend without regard to such person's claim.
I - do not think sudh powers should be given to any one; they might be abused.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The creditor has the
whole thirty days in which to -do it.

I do not think that is so, from a reading of the section. The notice shall be "within thirty days"; it does not say at least thirty days. It might be fifteen days after the notice, or two days after, and yet it would he within the thirty. As it is, the section is open to abuse.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Under the circumstances I move that the section be amended by striking out, in the second last line, the words "a time limited by the notice which shall be within," also striking out the bracket after the word "notice" on page 11.
What is meant by the words "prove his debt?"

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Those words are in the Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 30-final dividend and division of estate.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This is just an elaboration of a former section as to what the trustee has to do.
What is the meaning of "joint opinion?" Why not a majority?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This means that the trustee, on one hand, and the inspectors on the other, must agree.
Must it be unanimous on the part of the inspectors?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This simply means
that the majority of the inspectors must agree with the trustee; it must be a joint opinion.
It does not say that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is the meaning of the word "joint." I would as soon have the word "majority."
A joint opinion would mean an agreement between a majority of the trustees and the receiver.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There is only one
trustee. The idea that was intended hy the language employed was that the trustee, acting as one party, and the inspectors, who act by a majority, must agree.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 31-unpaid dividends paid to Receiver General.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Everything this section strikes out in the first fifteen lines of subsection 8 of section 37 of the Act is contained in section 30 which has been passed. There is no use of re-enacting it in subsection 8.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 32-no action for dividend unless improperly refused.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The only change which is made is the insertion of the
11 p.m. word " improperly " " If the trustee improperly refuses to pay" the court .may order him to pay, etc.

Take a case where a trustee, having received advice from a judge, refuses to pay. How can the judge afterwards order him to pay? Take the case we were discussing some time ago, where trustees received advice from the judge in relation to matters affecting the estate.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It would not be hbld then that the trustee had improperly refused to pay.
Assuming that the word " improperly " is added, and the trustee refuses to pay, acting on the advice of the judge.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not think he would then be improperly refusing to pay.

If the trustee, after being advised by the judge, is ordered by the

judge to pay, it would be a case of Caesar appealing to Caesar.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: If the trustee gets the direction of the court, he must comply with it.
The clause says that no action for dividends lies against the trustee. How will a man who has a claim for dividend enforce his claim if he has no action? How will he take his action?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The section provides
that if the trustee improperly refuses to pay any dividend the court may order him to pay it and also to pay out of his own money legal interest on the dividend for the time that it is withheld, and the costs of the application.
I know, but if he has no action.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He would not need to bring an action.
What is the meaning of the word "action"? The meaning of the word is "any legal process to enforce a claim."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, I would not say
that is the meaning of the word "action" in my province.
What is it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A motion to the court to compel a trustee to do an act would not be called an action. In the province of Ontario all actions are commenced by writ of summons, but this is a summary application to the court.
Would this clause mean that the man would not 'have an action against the trustee, but he might make a motion or petition before the court and ask to be paid?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
He would just go to
the bankruptcy judge, that is all, and get an order from the judge.

And make a motion
with respect to an application or petition. I think the word "action" in our courts means "any legal process adopted to enforce a claim whether by way of a summons or otherwise." Under this wording he would be debarred altogether.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I cannot understand
that. I think the clause is very clear. "No action shall be brought." That has quite a distinctive meaning in my mind, but it may not be so in my hon. friend's province. No action shall be brought but if the trustee

improperly refuses, the bankruptcy court may order him to pay.

Certainly, you can not
get into any other court.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
You cannot bring an
