action before the court.

I do not think the minister has quite answered my objection. Under the section 18 as amended, the authorized trustee may at any time apply to the courts for direction in any matter affecting the administration of the estate. If on the advice of the judge he improperly refuses to pay the dividend how is the bankruptcy judge afterwards to compel payment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the clause
carry?

No, we have had no
answer from the minister.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I did not hear the question, I was discussing another matter. Please repeat your question?

Under section 18, as
amended by us to-night, the trustee may apply to the courts for direction in relation in all matters concerning the estate. We will suppose he has received instruction and advice from the bankruptcy judge with regard to the payment of a dividend or refusal to pay. If he improperly refuses to pay, how can the petitioner, or the creditor, apply to the judge who has already given advice, to the trustee not to pay?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well it cannot be "improper" because whatever the trustee does, under the advice of the court, shall be his justification for so doing under the last two lines of section 16.
When a judge advises it, it is not improper.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think that is self-evident. But apart from that whatever directions the judge gives "shall bind, as well as justify, the subsequent consonant action of the trustee." That is pretty clear I think.

The point I am trying to make is that the judge has to advise and at the same time has to decide the very same question. He is advising the trustee and then has to decide the question as between the trustee and the creditor.

If I understand aright, the
wording of the clause is to avoid this situa-

tion: the Acting Solicitor General is adding the word "improperly" to the clause so that in case of prosecution the trustee would only have to say that he has not refused improperly because he was authorized to do so.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think that is the reason for adding it.
Is it fair?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think it is eminently fair.

I can easily appreciate that the trustee should be protected against actions which he is not liable for; but if he improperly refuses to pay a dividend, I think my hon. friend who has just spoken is correct when he asks what action could the creditor take if he refuses to carry out the judge's order.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Just apply to the court for an order to compel him.

I suppose there is an
appeal? That is the only way out of the impasse.
If he improperly refuses to carry out the judges order and no action lies, what other course is there to take?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The object of the section is to get away from actions, to stop them-
Surely.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: -and if the trustee improperly refuses the judge will order him to pay costs and damages. It is to expedite the thing and save expense.

Here is an ex-parte
judgment without the person knowing anything about it. It seems to me the word "improperly" is put in the wrong place in the section-that is a thing that ought to be tried. This is a section that provides absolute jurisdiction in some judge without the other man being heard at all. It seems to me there ought to be some notice given before an exemplary remedy of that kind should be applied.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
All applications and
motions under this Act are made in conformity with the provisions of the general rules which form a part of the Act. The general rules of practice provide for notice in every case.

Should we not insert
after the word "may" the words "on motion after notice."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Those words are not necessary, the general rules provide for it.
That may be the ease in some provinces but I do not know that it is the case in all of them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 33-remuneration of trustee.

I understand that this
amends and repeals the section which declares the trustee is only to receive five per cent?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No that is not repealed.
Well then we are providing for further remuneration to the trustee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: With respect to contests as between contributories, my hon. friend will remember that we provide in a previous section that the courts shall award costs to the trustee from the contributories but not from the estate. In the other case, it is in connection with the application of a bankrupt or authorized assignor for a discharge and the Act provides he must pay his own costs.
Section 40 refers to remuneration to the trustee. '

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, but we are not interfering with that.

The cases mentioned by the Acting Solicitor General are exceptional. The last sentence of the section says:
In the excepted cases the trustee's remuneration shall be fixed by the court.
In the two cases mentioned by the Acting Solicitor General the remuneration is fixed by the court and the general remuneration to the trustee will be fixed by the creditors.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is right.

So it leaves five per
cent.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, five per cent is all that comes out of the estate under paragraph (a) and paragraph (b). The first is where there is a contest between the contributories and they pay the cost. The second is where there is an application by a bankrupt for a discharge from the court and the estate does not pay the cost.

If there were a probability of this Bill being disposed of in a few minutes I would not make the suggestion I am about to make. But it is now a quarter past eleven o'clock and I think we are

all anxious to get into better habits of sitting. I would therefore suggest to my hon. friend that he should let the committee rise and report progress. I am not desiring to delay his Bill, hut I am told it will occupy some considerable time.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
If that is the general
desire of the committee well and good, but I thought probably it would be the desire of the committee to go ahead with the Bill and get rid of it.

It is not the general
desire.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
If the committee is
anxious to stop now I have no objection. My own wish, if it meets with the approval of the committee, would be to go ahead with the Bill. I do not think there is much contention about the rest of the measure.
Man proposes but-
The section provides in effect that the remuneration shall be decided by "a majority of the creditors present". Should it not read "a majority of those creditors present"?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not quite catch the distinction.	[DOT]
As the section is drafted it might require a majority of all persons who have claims against the estate to be present, whereas what you mean is a majority of those creditors present.
I think instead of using this form it would be far better English if it read "a majority of the creditors who are present".

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I was going to move to amend it to read "a majority of the creditors who are present", but my adviser says that it is bad English.

Surely it is not
suggested that the phrase "who are. present" is bad English?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am told that the word "majority" is a collective noun, and therefore the expression "who are" is bad English.

Mr. Chairman, I
move that the word "the" in line 44 be struck out and the word "those" be inserted in lieu thereof.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The clause has been revised by very eminent counsel and I should not like to change the language employed unless I was very sure there was something wrong with it.
If I understand my hon. friend correctly, his contention is that as the clause reads now all the creditors would have to be present?
A majority of all the creditors.
If the majority of the creditors were not present this clause would not have application.
That is exactly the point. "The" creditors means all the creditors of the estate. It should read "a majority of those creditors present".
If you strike out the word "the" you make it quite plain.
Substitute "those".
Strike out the word "the".

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I move to amend clause 33 by striking out the word "the" before the word "creditors" in the 44th line.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 34-discharge of trustee, etc.:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This is an elaboration of the present section with very slight additions. There is no provision in the old section for a discharge where another trustee has been appointed and the account is satisfactory. There are provisions here for discharge when accounts are approved and two years have elapsed after the final dividend.
I move to amend subsection 5 by adding after the word "in" in line 33 the following words: "or done under authority of".

The section says that it shall not be deemed to be a legal discharge of the trustee from the results of fraud or any fraudulent breach of trust. I suppose that is by the trustee, but it does not say so.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is the only thing he would be liable for, is it not?
It does not say so.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: But that is the law.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

In the case of a trustee replaced by a majority of the creditors how do you provide for payment of his fee? I understand that in a general way a trustee is paid certain fees in the discretion of the creditors, although sometimes the fees are fixed by the court. I do not think that in the case of a trustee being replaced by another trustee he should have to depend

for payment of his fees on the same creditors who have dismissed him without cause.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: When a trustee is removed, if he does not desire to accept the remuneration which the creditors vote, he may apply to the court to have his remuneration fixed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I note what seems
to be an anomaly in line 10; " and of the claimed sufficient cause." The French version has it: " et de la cause suffisante alleguee," .which seems to me to convey more fully the meaning intended.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think that "alleged" would he better. I move that the word " alleged " be substituted for the word " claimed " in line 10 of section 34.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 35-power of chairman of creditors' meeting to admit or reject proof.

There seems to be an anomaly in this clause. It is provided that the chairman of the meeting may accept a telegram coming from Richford, Vermont, 60 miles from Montreal, whereas if it came from Victoria he would not have the right to act upon it. If you are going to have the provision at all you should make it logical by establishing it on the basis of distance from the place where the meeting is being held.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This provision is for the convenience of foreign creditors doing business in Canada, particularly those of Great Britain who requested it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 38-secured creditor to value securities.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The only change in this section is in regard to the identification of property by a creditor who claims security on individual property. In the case, for instance, of a cafe where there are fifty tables on twenty of which security is claimed, the difficulty has been to require the identification of the particular tables. This provision has been inserted to facilitate matters in that respect.
Does this section apply to the banks as well as to individuals?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: To all creditors who claim to be secured.

Under' the Windingup Act, it has been held that a creditor who is secured on a property may elect to take that property and abandon his claim upon the estate. Is this amendment intended to vary the law in that regard?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 39-priority of claims.
Will this apply to the province of Quebec? In that province there is a Workmen's Compensation Act, but no board.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well, we ought to make that sufficiently broad. I move that the words " or under any Workmen's Compensation Act " be added after the word " board " on line 41.

As I understand the
law of Ontario, an employer who is found liable to a workman, pays that money, not to the workmen, pays the Compensation Board which, in turn, hands it over to the workman. I think I am right in that. Under our law in Quebec, the debt is a debt which is paid directly to the workman or, in case of death, to the workman's representatives.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Under this clause,
claims would be paid in the following order of priority:	First would come fees of the
trustees; second, the costs of the first executive creditor, third, wages, salaries, commissions and any damages awarded by any Workmen's Compensation Board or Workmen's Compensation Act.
Amendment (Mr. Guthrie) agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 40-continued occupation of leased premises by trustee.

Does the Solicitor Gentral not think that this notice is very short? Supposing this should occur in winter, and in January the trustee gives a month's notice that he is going to vacate the premises in February, when premises are rented from the first of May. That is not fair. In Quebec-and I suppose the same is true throughout the re'st of Canada-our leases are generally yearly from the first of May in one year to the first of May in the following year. Supposing a trustee takes possession of premises under the law, and when he is through with his work, say in January, he gives one month's notice that he is going to vacate the premises-is that the meaning of the clause?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We went into these
clauses very carefully when the Act was being passed, and the disposition of both the committee and the House was to treat, as some thought, hardly the rights of landlords as compared with the rights of creditors. I cannot say for myself that I think there is any harshness in this clause. The trustee has a right to continue in possession of leased premises for so long as he shall require the premises for the trust estate. The clause states further:
The trustee may surrender possession at any time tout if he shall occupy for three months or more beyond the date of the making of the receiving order or authorized assignment the landlord shall be entitled to receive one month's notice in writing of the trustee's intention to surrender possession or one month's rent in lieu thereof.
That, in Ontario, would be considered a fair and reasonable notice.
Not with us in Quebec.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I understand that in
Quebec leases are for longer terms than in Ontario.
Leases in Quebec are usually for one year.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The clause continues:
After the trustee surrenders possession such of the landlord's rights as are based upon actual occupation by the trustee shall cease.
I do not think that is unreasonable, having application at least to eight of the provinces of Canada.

This would constitute a rather unfair hardship to landlords in Quebec, where leases are made for a term which is usually at least a year. Where tenants can be found, as a rule, only between February 1 and May 1, which is the leasing period in Quebec, it is a hardship to order a landlord to allow a trustee to stay on the premises, say until August 1, then to give one month's notice and to be able to get out of the premises, say September 1. Under the law of Quebec, if there is no writing and the rent is so much a year, a yearly lease is presumed, and unless one party gives to the other party notice of intention to terminate, the lease runs on from year to year, terminable only on three months' notice. That is the usual custom with us. You are departing from that reasonable custom here; you are giving the trustee the right to stay in the premises as long as he needs them and then to clear out on one month's notice or one month's rent in lieu of notice. According

to our custom, which may be right or wrong, that causes a hardship to a landlord by having, in the autumn months, his premises thrown on his hands on one month's notice when he may not be able to rent those premises until next May, although the insolvency may have occurred in April and the trustee continued in possession of the premises during April, May, June and July.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We will let clauses 40, 41, 42 and 43 stand.

I would ask the minister to consider these clauses again before coming back to the committee. The question arises whether these clauses are legal or not, because there is no doubt that under them we are doing away with civil and property rights of the provinces. In our province we have specific laws concerning these matters. Has this Parliament the right to do away with them? I should like the Solicitor General, in consultation with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), to consider this question and to tell us about it when this Bill comes again before the committee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We have had many consultations with many eminent members of the bar in Quebec and Ontario. These and similar clauses were inserted and we were assured that they were quite within our powers.

I think the one month's notice is too short. The notice ought to be three months. That is what we used to have in the Assignment Act in Ontario and in the Winding-up Act.
Section stands.
On section 47-search warrants:

This section provides that the court may by warrant order the breaking open of any place where the debtor is believed to be. Suppose he happens to be in a hotel. What is the good of breaking open the door? We do not want him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
They might want to
examine him or to serve him with process.
They do not serve a man with process by breaking down the door and handing him a document. That is an entirely new way.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This is simply to give full power.

Why not say "the breaking open of any building or place where

any part of the property of the debtor is believed to be?"

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This is from the English Act. It has been found to be necessary because some debtors evade service and hide and lock themselves in.
We have proceedings to reach him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I suppose they have in England.

In our province the judge will provide a method for service in the case of a man who is constantly evading it. He can give the bailiff instructions to tack the notice on the door or proceed in some such fashion. We avoid this breaking in.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It cannot be done without the sanction of the court.
It is not considered polite to break open a door and hand a man a visiting card.

There is another point. This clause provides that certain things shall be done as is provided by the Criminal Code. By what officials will these things be done? Not by civil bailiff. By constables, I suppose?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The general rules attached to the Act prescribe that a process of this kind shall be executed by the sheriff.
Would that cover the sheriff's deputy?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The sheriff's officers.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 48-who may act for corporations, firms and lunatics:
In our province the lunatic has a curator not only for his property but for his person.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The section says "or by the guardian or curator of his property."

You say "a lunatic may act by his committee or by the guardian or curator of his property." It does seem to me that the inference to be drawn from the law is that the committee is a person in charge of the lunatic and that the curator or guardian is in possession of the property of the lunatic, but not responsible for the lunatic himself, at least, not his legal representative. In our province "curator" is the title of the person who acts for a lunatic. He is the guardian
so to speak, not only of the property of the lunatic, but also of his person. I think it would be better to say "act by his committee or curator."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I move to insert after the word "committee" at the end of the 37th line on page 16 of the Bill the words "or curator."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 49-where a body of persons and court given alternative powers, court to await prior action:
What does that mean?

Talleyrand once said that the object of language was to conceal thought, the terms in which this Bill is couched make one think, not exactly like Talleyrand that the object has been to conceal thought, but to surround it with as many words as possible in order that one should have to exercise one's mind in order to find out exactly what the clauses mean.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Power is given here to a body of persons to take certain action or to decide a certain action. The power to apply to the court is a subsequent proceeding. The court will not act until it has satisfactory proof of prior application to such body of persons and of that body's refusal of the application. To my mind the language is fairly clear, though it is a bit involved, because it has to cover a great deal. There must be proof to the satisfaction of the court that application was first made to the creditors, and that they have refused or omitted to act, before the court will entertain the application.

I would direct attention to the word "alternatively" in line 43. It would almost seem to me that that clause meant that there was a sort of dual control-this body of persons being given power or authority, and the court being given like power or authority alternatively-or that power was in both the body of persons and in the court.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Oh, no.
Then I think my opening remarks on this section were very much in point.
Is this section taken from the English Act?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The object is to save
costs, and my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice thinks the section is well worded-

I have no doubt he
thinks so.

I am sure the section
must appeal to the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 50-Penalty for removing, attempting or counselling removal of debtor's goods without notice.

Does the minister think this is a good clause? I do not think we should change our Criminal Code in any way. The Criminal Code is hard enough to understand as it is, without having special clauses interfering with its general principles. Why should colour of right, in respect of a case, not be a defence? That is essential.

This section undermines
our criminal law.

I said earlier in the
evening that this Bill would override our provincial civil laws, and now I find it is doing away with our criminal laws.

We had section 97 when the Act first became law two years ago, and it was such a fool section that we afterwards repealed it. The minister will remember how we on this side of the House objected to it at the time. We had section 96 and section 98, but no section 97; and it appears to me that those in authority simply want to insert something now to fill in the hiatus, and they are enacting something which is to my mind as much a fool section as the old section 97.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We have already passed to-night a section that provides that where any one claims a lien on goods, he shall not remove the goods for a period of fifteen days. This merely provides that if he does so in contravention of that section, 22, he shall be liable to a penalty and shall not be allowed to set up any defence of colour of right.
Why not?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Because he is transgressing the strict letter of the law. The law must be obeyed,- and it says that he shall not remove the goods for fifteen days. If he deliberately breaks the law-
It is for the court to say whether he deliberately breaks it or not.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: -then he shall not be allowed to plead colour of right.

Suppose I am prosecuted under this section, and I wish to plead

colour of right as a defence, and the Crown objects. Does not the Minister of Justice think that it would be a perfectly good answer to say that we have criminal laws and that outside of the Criminal Code there cannot be any special law taking away the rights of citizens as protected by the criminal laws of the country?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Yes, we can override
the Criminal Code.

I have some experience in the criminal courts, and while
12 m. I do not know what the Solicitor General would decide if he were a presiding judge, I know that most judges would say, the Criminal Code covers all these offences.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We depart from the
Criminal Code in almost every Act we pass. In the Opium and Drug Act and the Migratory Birds Act which we had under discussion to-day we depart from it, and this is the case in almost every Act which imposes penalties.

This is a question of
theft. This is a ease where we can proceed against a party under the old larceny law.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Not if he is the owner
of the goods.
He is not the owner when the receiver takes possession.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He is the owner and he is compelled to leave them there, under the law we have enacted to-night, for fifteen days, to give the trustee a chance to see -whether he has title. If you do not obey the plain letter of the law, and you deliberately take the goods away, there is a penalty. People must obey the law. My hon. friend refers to larceny. Suppose you were the owner of the goods; where would there be any larceny?

My hon. friend knows
that there are sections in the Criminal Code dealing with, cases of that kind, where a man can steal from himself.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Where I sell a table
and take a lien note, complying with some provincial law, if the condition on which the table was sold becomes forfeited and I want to take possession of the table-
You replevy it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I make an assignment,
and I have to wait fifteen days before I can get the table. If I did take the table

away before fifteen days I could not be prosecuted for larceny if I were the owner.

If I recollect my
. criminal law, I think that if a thing is in the hands of the court, in the hands of the bailiff or of the trustee, any man, even if he were the owner, who took possession of it would be guilty of a criminal offence. I should like to hear the Minister of Justice on that point.
The minister is horror-stricken. He has not spoken this evening.

What would happen if
the party claiming the property went to the civil court and got an order to replevy?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It would not be good
against the Bankruptcy Act. Civil provisions in the provincial law have been overridden by provisions in the Bankruptcy Act, and cases from Quebec on that question were decided by the Privy Council, where it was held that because the procedure of the province of Quebec required certain things, and the old Insolvency Act overrode those provisions, the Insolvency Act was ultra vires and unconstitutional. It was held, however, that this Parliament had a perfect right to override the civil procedure of Quebec in regard to anything necessary or incidental to the law of bankruptcy or insolvency.
But has this Parliament the special right to create offences in contradiction to the provisions of the Criminal Code?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Without amending the
Criminal Code?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Yes, we could say
"notwithstanding anything in the Criminal Code."
The section declares that the party who contravenes it is liable to a fine of $5,000 or to two years' imprisonment. Would the minister be good enough to tell me why $5,000 is provided as a penalty?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Suppose we strike out this "colour of right" to satisfy my hon. friend?
To satisfy justice.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Strike out "colour of right shall not be a defence and." The clause will then read:
In proceedings under this section any person counselling or directing the offence involved-
And so forth.
I think the $5,000 penalty is excessive and that the penalty should be "not exceeding one thousand dollars."

Might I suggest to the Acting Solicitor General that he might just as well strike out that last sentence because is not an accessory before the fact a person who does exactly what is set out in terms in the last sentence of this section? An accessory before the fact is, if I remember correctly, liable to the penalty and is held guilty of the offence, and a person who counsels or abets before the commission of an offence, even though he does not participate in' the offence itself, is an accessory before the fact.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He is a principal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I quite agree, after consultation with the Solitictor General, that it should come out because the man that counsels or abets, and all the rest of it, is not merely an accessory before the fact but is a principal.
Is a party to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, a party.

The penalty of $5,000 is
excessive.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We will have to stick to it.
I may say that throughout the Act wherever a fine is imposed it is in every case $1,000 or two years' imprisonment or both. I think that is the wording in different sections of the Bill.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well, cases have arisen where goods to the extent of $25,000 have been removed. In one case, I think, it was shoe machinery that was taken out; in another case very expensive printing presses were removed. The judge would apportion that.

But we should make the change in order to maintain the symmetry of the penalties, if I may so describe it. We find in other sections that bankrupts who contravene the law are liable to a fine of $1,000 or two years' imprisonment, or both. Why not fix the penalty in this case at $1,000?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It is too little for a big affair. I move that the words from "in proceedings", line 19, to the end of the section be struck out.

speakerposition: topic
Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Guthrie moves to further amend clause 50 by striking out from the end thereof the following words:
In proceedings under this section colour of right shall not he a defence and any person counselling or directing the offence involved shall, in the event of its commission by the person counselled or directed, he liable to conviction of the offence cumulatively with the actual offender, even though such person counselling or directing was not an actual participant in the offence."
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.
On section 51-liability of officer, director or agent of company.

Is that participation to be real or just statutory or technical? For instance, a director or official of the company may technically participate in an act but in reality he does not. Would he be criminally responsible under this clause, for technical participation in an act?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think the participation would have to be actual participation.

Why not put in the
word "actual?"

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think it means actual.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Department of .health-salaries, $155,612.50.

May I ask when we will get a review of the work of this department? It spends about a million dollars a year, it has been in existence two years or nearly that, and we know practically nothing about it at the present time.
Perhaps the minister will give a comprehensive review such as he gave on immigration the other day when the House was enlightened for some little time.

We will find that our
health is not improved.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I may state in reply to the hon.- member for Muskoka that if there is an opportunity, when we are dealing with the Health Estimates, I will make a statement regarding some of the activities of the department. In the meantime, as it is pretty late, I would move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.
On the motion of the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 12.15 a.m.

Wednesday, May 4, 1921.
